High blood pressure usually has no warning signs or symptoms, which is why it is often called the "silent killer".
The Silent Nature of Hypertension
No physical clues: Most people with high blood pressure feel completely normal and do not know they have it.
Regular checks needed: You must get your blood pressure measured by a healthcare provider or home monitor to know your status.
Hidden damage: Untreated high blood pressure can still damage your heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes over time without you feeling sick.

Headaches: Early-morning dull headaches, especially at the back of the head.
Vision changes: Blurred vision or eye strain.
Dizziness: Feeling lightheaded, woozy, or unsteady.
Fatigue: Feeling unusually exhausted because your heart works harder to pump blood.
Nosebleeds: Frequent or sudden nosebleeds.
Pounding: A rhythmic thumping sensation in your ears, neck, or chest.
Hypertensive Emergency Symptoms

Chest pain or tightness
Severe, sudden headache
Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Confusion or trouble speaking
Sudden weakness, numbness, or facial drooping (signs of stroke)

Blood pressure is recorded as two numbers. The top number is systolic pressure (when the heart beats), and the bottom number is diastolic pressure (when the heart rests between beats).
Blood Pressure Categories

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure your blood sugar levels.
According to the American Diabetes Association, doctors use these main blood tests for a diagnosis:
Diagnostic Blood Tests
A1C Test: Measures your average blood sugar over the past two to three months. A result of 6.5% or higher on two separate tests means you have diabetes. No fasting is required.
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: Measures your blood sugar after you do not eat or drink anything except water for at least eight hours. A result of 126 mg/dL or higher means you have diabetes.
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): Measures your blood sugar two hours after you drink a special sweet liquid. A level of 200 mg/dL or higher confirms diabetes.
Random Plasma Glucose Test: Checks your blood sugar at any time when you have severe diabetes symptoms. A level of 200 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.
Confirmation
Doctors usually repeat an abnormal test on a second day to confirm the diagnosis, unless you have very high blood sugar or clear, classic symptoms.

GLP-1 receptor agonists: These are injectable drugs (like semaglutide) that boost insulin, lower blood sugar, and help with weight loss.

Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): These pills improve your body's sensitivity to insulin.
Insulin: If other drugs do not work well enough, you can inject synthetic insulin using a pen, syringe, or pump.
Surgical Options

No early warnings: You can have high blood pressure for years without knowing it while it damages your heart, brain, and kidneys.

Severe, sudden headache
Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Chest pain or tightness
Sudden vision changes or blurry vision

Signs of a stroke (slurred speech, facial drooping, or weakness on one side)

Comorbidity-Driven Selection: Major guidelines (such as the American Diabetes Association) recommend starting SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 RAs early—either with metformin or as initial therapy—if the patient has established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), heart failure, or chronic kidney disease (CKD).

Combination Therapy: Many patients with high-risk cardiorenal disease eventually take both classes together for synergistic protection.

High blood pressure (hypertension) treatment options combine heart-healthy lifestyle changes and first-line prescription medications.
Lifestyle Changes
DASH Diet: Eat more fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while lowering sodium (salt) intake.
Physical Activity: Get regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, to strengthen the heart.
Weight Management: Work toward or maintain a healthy body weight.
Limit Alcohol: Reduce alcohol consumption to no more than one drink per day for women or two drinks per day for men.
Quit Smoking: Stop smoking or vaping to prevent blood vessel narrowing and elevated heart rates.
Stress and Sleep: Manage chronic stress and aim for consistent, quality sleep.
First-Line Medications
Doctors typically select from four main classes of prescription drugs:
ACE Inhibitors: Block natural chemicals that tighten blood vessels (examples: lisinopril, benazepril).
Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Relax blood vessels by blocking specific hormone receptors (examples: losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Relax and widen artery walls (examples: amlodipine, diltiazem).
Thiazide Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the body flush out excess sodium and water (examples: chlorthalidone, hydrochlorothiazide).
Additional or Combo Options
Beta-Blockers: Lower heart rate and cardiac workload.
Combination Therapy: Many people—especially those with Stage 2 hypertension—require two or more medications from different classes to reach a goal of under 130/80 mmHg.

Both ACE inhibitors and ARBs (Angiotensin Receptor Blockers) are recommended as equal class-I first-line treatments for high blood pressure, though are increasingly favored due to a lower risk of side effects.
How They Work
ACE inhibitors (ending in -pril, such as lisinopril and enalapril) block the body from producing angiotensin II, a chemical that narrows blood vessels.
ARBs (ending in -sartan, such as losartan and valsartan) block angiotensin II receptors directly, keeping the chemical from binding and tightening blood vessels.
Efficacy (Effectiveness)
Blood Pressure & Outcomes: Large-scale studies, including the analysis of nearly 3 million patients, show that both drug classes are equally effective at lowering blood pressure and preventing major cardiovascular events like heart attacks and strokes.
Side Effects and Tolerability
ACE inhibitors have a higher rate of side effects, most notably a persistent dry cough (affecting roughly 20% of users) and a rare, potentially serious swelling of the face or tongue known as angioedema (which occurs more frequently in African American patients).
ARBs provide a much better safety and tolerability profile with significantly lower rates of discontinuation, cough, and .
Shared risks: Both classes can raise blood potassium levels (hyperkalemia) and must be combined with each other or taken during pregnancy.

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over years, and many people do not notice symptoms in the early stages.
Frequent urination: Excess sugar builds up in the blood, and your kidneys try to flush it out by producing more urine (especially at night).
Increased thirst and dry mouth: Because you are losing more fluids through frequent urination, you feel constantly dehydrated and thirsty.
Fatigue and weakness: Your cells cannot absorb glucose properly for energy, leaving you unusually tired.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar can cause fluid to shift and swell the lenses of your eyes, making it hard to focus.
Slow-healing cuts and sores: High blood sugar damages blood vessels and impairs circulation, slowing down your body's ability to repair wounds.
Tingling or numbness: High glucose levels can damage peripheral nerves (neuropathy), often causing a pins-and-needles feeling or numbness in the hands or feet.
Darkened skin patches: A condition called acanthosis nigricans causes velvety, dark patches of skin in body folds like the neck, armpits, or groin, which signals strong insulin resistance.
Frequent infections: Higher blood sugar weakens the immune system, leading to recurring urinary tract infections (UTIs) or yeast infections.
Unexplained weight changes: Your body may start burning fat and muscle for fuel if it cannot use glucose properly, leading to weight loss, though some people experience weight gain.
You can read more about risk factors and progression through the Mayo Clinic or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure your blood sugar or average glucose levels.
According to guidelines from the American Diabetes Association and the Mayo Clinic, type 2 diabetes is confirmed if you meet any of the following thresholds:
A1C Test (Glycated Hemoglobin): 6.5% or higher (measures average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months; no fasting required).
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: 126 mg/dL or higher (taken in the morning after at least an 8-hour fast without food or drink except water).
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): 200 mg/dL or higher (measured 2 hours after drinking a 75-gram glucose solution).
Random Plasma Glucose Test: 200 mg/dL or higher (taken at any time of day, used if you have classic symptoms of high blood sugar like frequent urination or extreme thirst).
Repeat Testing: Except in cases of severe symptoms with a high random glucose reading, doctors typically confirm the result by repeating one of the diagnostic tests on a subsequent day.
Prediabetes Range: If your results fall between an A1C of 5.7%–6.4%, a fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dL, or an OGTT of 140–199 mg/dL, it indicates prediabetes.
Screening Recommendations: Routine screening is recommended for adults starting at age 35, or earlier if you have risk factors such as overweight or obesity, a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure, or a history of gestational diabetes.

High blood pressure (hypertension) is diagnosed when your blood pressure readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.
Doctors use the guidelines from the American Heart Association to classify blood pressure levels:
Normal: Less than 120 / under 80 mm Hg
Elevated: 120–129 / under 80 mm Hg
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130–139 / 80–89 mm Hg
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140 or higher / 90 or higher mm Hg
Hypertensive Crisis (Emergency): Higher than 180 and/or higher than 120 mm Hg
Systolic (top number): Measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart beats.
Diastolic (bottom number): Measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart rests between beats.
A reading above 180/120 mm Hg requires waiting a few minutes and retesting. If it remains this high and you have warning signs like chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, or vision changes, call 911 immediately. Otherwise, contact your doctor right away.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is treated using a combination of lifestyle modifications and prescription medications, with a general blood pressure target of less than 130/80 mmHg.
Non-pharmacologic changes are the foundation of treatment and can help lower blood pressure or reduce the number of medications needed:
Dietary Changes: Follow the DASH (Diet Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet, which focuses on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy.
Sodium Reduction: Limit daily sodium intake to less than 1,500 mg per day.
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise (such as brisk walking) for at least 150 minutes per week.
Weight Management: Achieve and maintain a healthy weight.
Substance Limits: Limit alcohol consumption and quit smoking.
Sleep and Stress: Prioritize good sleep hygiene and manage stress.
When lifestyle changes are not enough—or immediately for Stage 2 hypertension (140/90 mmHg or higher) or high-risk patients—doctors prescribe one or more of these first-line drug classes:
Angiotensin-Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Relax blood vessels by blocking a hormone called angiotensin (e.g., losartan, valsartan); often favored if you have diabetes or kidney disease.
ACE Inhibitors: Prevent blood vessels from narrowing by stopping angiotensin production (e.g., lisinopril, enalapril).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells to let vessels relax (e.g., amlodipine, nifedipine).
Thiazide Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the body get rid of excess sodium and water (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone).
If blood pressure goals are not met with a single drug, providers often combine two or more medications at lower doses rather than raising to a high single dose. Other classes include:
Beta-Blockers: Slow the heart rate and reduce the force of pumping (e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol).
Mineralocorticoid/Aldosterone Antagonists: Used for resistant hypertension (e.g., spironolactone).
Alpha-Blockers and Vasodilators: Relax blood vessel walls when other options need supplementation.
You can read more detailed treatment guidelines through the Mayo Clinic High Blood Pressure Guide or review medication classes via the American Heart Association.

Nasal congestion or upper respiratory symptoms
Back or joint pain
Contact a doctor or seek immediate medical care if you experience any of these severe reactions:

Both Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs) are considered equivalent, effective first-line treatments for high blood pressure, though large observational studies show that ARBs offer similar cardiovascular protection with a lower rate of side effects.
Effectiveness: Both drug classes lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events (like heart attacks and strokes) just as effectively .
Mechanism of Action:
Side Effects & Tolerability:
Shared Side Effects: Both classes can cause elevated potassium levels ( ), dizziness or fatigue from low blood pressure ( ), and temporary changes in kidney function.
Contraindications: Both drug classes are strictly unsafe during pregnancy (teratogenic) and should be avoided or closely monitored in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis . They should never be combined with each other due to a higher risk of kidney injury and low blood pressure without extra benefit.
Historical Standard: ACE inhibitors have a longer clinical history and older trial data, which is why historical medical guidelines frequently recommended them first .
Current Shift: Modern data—including a massive international study of over 3 million patients published via and the American Heart Association—support initiating treatment with ARBs because of their superior tolerability profile.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which forces the right side of the heart to work harder and leads to reduced oxygen and blood flow.
Shortness of breath (dyspnea): Often starts during physical activity like climbing stairs or exercising, and can eventually happen even at rest.
Fatigue and weakness: Feeling unusually tired or drained during normal daily tasks.
Chest pain or pressure: Caused by the extra strain on the heart muscle.
Dizziness or lightheadedness: Especially when standing up or exerting yourself.
Fainting (syncope): Occurs as heart strain and blood flow limitations become more severe.
Heart palpitations: A fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat.
Swelling (edema): Fluid buildup in the ankles, feet, legs, or abdomen due to heart strain.
Cyanosis: A bluish or grayish tint to the lips, fingers, or skin from low oxygen levels.
PAH symptoms are often mild or nonexistent in the early stages and mimic other heart or lung conditions. As the disease progresses, daily activities become much harder.
You should seek emergency medical care if you experience:
Fainting or blacking out
A fast heart rate that will not slow down
Severe or sudden chest pain
Shortness of breath that does not go away with rest

Early signs of type 2 diabetes often develop slowly over years and include frequent urination, increased thirst, persistent fatigue, and blurred vision.
Frequent urination (polyuria): High blood sugar forces your kidneys to work overtime to filter and flush out the excess glucose, which pulls fluids from your tissues and makes you visit the restroom more often, including at night.
Excessive thirst (polydipsia): Because you are losing more fluids through frequent urination, you often feel unusually thirsty and have a dry mouth.
Persistent fatigue: When your cells cannot properly absorb glucose due to insulin resistance, your body lacks its main source of energy.
Blurred vision: Fluctuating blood sugar levels can cause fluid to shift into the lenses of your eyes, temporarily changing their shape and making it hard to focus.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: High blood sugar levels impair circulation and weaken your immune response, making minor wounds take much longer to heal.
Tingling or numbness: Peripheral neuropathy can cause a "pins and needles" sensation, burning, or numbness in your hands, feet, legs, or arms.
Darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin—frequently found in folds like the neck, armpits, or groin—can signal underlying insulin resistance.
Increased hunger or weight changes: You may feel hungrier shortly after eating because energy isn't reaching your cells, or experience unexplained weight changes.
Frequent infections: Higher glucose levels create an environment where yeast and bacteria thrive, leading to recurring urinary tract infections (UTIs) or yeast infections.
Because many early symptoms are subtle or easy to dismiss, type 2 diabetes is confirmed through simple blood work ordered by a healthcare provider, such as:
Fasting plasma glucose test
Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) test (measures average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months)
Random plasma glucose test

Both ACE (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme) inhibitors and ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers) are considered equivalent first-line treatments for high blood pressure (hypertension).
Effectiveness: Both classes target the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) to relax blood vessels, lower blood pressure, and protect the heart and kidneys . Large studies show they have essentially identical long-term effectiveness in preventing major cardiovascular events like heart attacks and strokes.
Shared Contraindications: Neither class is safe to use during pregnancy (due to the risk of birth defects), and they should never be combined together due to increased risks of high potassium and kidney damage.
Side Effects (Cough): ACE inhibitors (such as lisinopril or enalapril) block the breakdown of bradykinin, which causes a persistent, dry, nagging cough in about 5% to 20% of users. ARBs (such as losartan or valsartan) do not affect bradykinin and rarely cause this cough.
Angioedema: ACE inhibitors carry a small risk of angioedema (swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat), which happens more often in individuals of African descent. ARBs have a much lower risk.
Track Record vs. Cost: ACE inhibitors have a longer clinical history and extensive trial data, while ARBs generally offer superior patient tolerability (fewer discontinuations) and are now widely available as affordable generics.
Many clinicians lean toward ARBs first because patients tolerate them better with fewer side effects. However, if you already take an ACE inhibitor like lisinopril and are doing well without a cough, there is usually no need to switch. If a dry cough develops on an ACE inhibitor, doctors typically transition the patient directly to an ARB.

Early signs of type 2 diabetes often develop slowly over months or years, making them easy to miss. According to the Mayo Clinic and the Cleveland Clinic, common early warning signs include:
Core Symptoms
Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar forces your kidneys to work overtime to filter and absorb excess glucose, causing you to pee more often—especially at night—and feel constantly thirsty.
Fatigue and weakness: When your cells cannot effectively absorb glucose for energy, you may experience persistent exhaustion, brain fog, or low energy.
Increased hunger: You may feel hungry shortly after eating because your body's cells are starved of the fuel they need.
Blurred vision: Excess sugar in the blood can cause fluid to shift into the lenses of your eyes, temporarily changing their shape and making your vision fuzzy.
Slow-healing sores or frequent infections: High blood sugar impairs circulation and weakens immune responses, making cuts, bruises, skin infections, urinary tract infections (UTIs), or yeast infections take longer to heal.
Tingling or numbness: Peripheral nerve damage from high blood sugar can cause a pins-and-needles sensation, burning, or numbness in the hands or feet.
Darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin—frequently appearing on the neck, armpits, or groin—can be an early marker of insulin resistance.
Unexplained weight changes: Some individuals experience sudden, unintended weight loss as the body starts burning fat and muscle for energy, while others may experience weight gain linked to insulin resistance.
If you or someone you know is experiencing these symptoms, the safest next step is to schedule a visit with a doctor for a simple blood test (such as a fasting blood glucose or A1c test) to get an accurate diagnosis. Type 2 diabetes treatment relies on a combination of lifestyle changes, oral or injectable medications, and organ-protection strategies tailored to your specific health profile.
1. Foundation: Lifestyle Modifications
Nutrition: Focus on whole foods like the Mediterranean diet, high-fiber vegetables, and limited processed sugars.
Physical Activity: Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic exercise per week plus 2 to 3 sessions of strength training.
Weight Management: Achieving a 5% to 7% (or higher) weight reduction can significantly improve insulin sensitivity and glucose control.
Sleep and Stress: Prioritize 7 to 8 hours of sleep nightly and manage stress through daily movement and recovery habits.
2. Oral and Injectable Medications
Current guidelines from organizations like the American Diabetes Association emphasize choosing medications based on your whole health (such as heart or kidney status) rather than just blood sugar numbers alone:
Metformin: Often prescribed as a trusted, low-cost first-line oral pill to improve how your body handles insulin.
SGLT2 Inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin): Pills that help the kidneys remove extra glucose through urine while offering major protective benefits for the heart and kidneys.
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs (e.g., semaglutide, tirzepatide): Weekly injections that boost insulin release, slow digestion, support substantial weight loss, and protect cardiovascular health.
Other Oral Options: Including DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins), sulfonylureas, or thiazolidinediones, which may be added or used depending on individual tolerance and target goals.
Insulin Therapy: Considered if blood sugar remains high despite other treatments, or introduced earlier in cases of severe hyperglycemia. Continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) are widely recommended to track real-time levels safely.

Severe headaches or a feeling of a pounding in the head, neck, or ears

Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Vision changes, such as blurred vision or eye pain

Nosebleeds or blood spots in the eyes

Blood pressure is considered high (hypertension) when it is consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg according to the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Blood Pressure Categories
Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg systolic (top number) and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic (bottom number).
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic.
Stage 1 Hypertension (High): 130–139 mm Hg systolic or 80–89 mm Hg diastolic.
Stage 2 Hypertension (High): 140 mm Hg or higher systolic, or 90 mm Hg or higher diastolic.
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic.
Understanding the Numbers
Systolic (top number): Measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart beats.
Diastolic (lower number): Measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart rests between beats.
You can be diagnosed with high blood pressure if either number meets the threshold for Stage 1 or Stage 2, even if the other number is normal.
What to Do in a Crisis
Severe Hypertension without symptoms: Recheck your blood pressure after a few minutes. If it remains over 180/120 mm Hg, contact your doctor immediately.
Hypertensive Emergency (with symptoms): If a reading over 180/120 mm Hg is accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, sudden confusion, vision changes, or numbness, call 911 immediately.

Treatment options for high blood pressure (hypertension) include heart-healthy lifestyle modifications and prescription medications, as outlined by the Mayo Clinic and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.
Lifestyle Modifications
DASH Diet: Eat a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fat.
Sodium Reduction: Limit daily sodium intake to 1,500 mg or less (or under 2,300 mg maximum).
Physical Activity: Get about 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (such as brisk walking) per week.
Weight Management: Lose or maintain a healthy body weight if you are overweight.
Habits: Quit smoking, limit alcohol consumption, manage chronic stress, and get 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night.
First-Line Medications
Doctors often prescribe one or more of these standard drug classes, detailed by the American Heart Association:
ACE Inhibitors: Help blood vessels relax and widen (e.g., Lisinopril, Enalapril).
Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Block chemicals that constrict blood vessels, often preferred to protect the kidneys (e.g., Losartan, Valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel cells to lower pressure (e.g., Amlodipine, Diltiazem).
Thiazide Diuretics: "Water pills" that help the body get rid of excess sodium and water (e.g., Chlorthalidone, Hydrochlorothiazide).
Additional & Combination Options
Beta-Blockers: Often used if you have coexisting heart conditions, heart failure, or arrhythmias (e.g., Metoprolol, Carvedilol).
Other Agents: Alpha-blockers, central-acting agents, or vasodilators may be added if blood pressure remains uncontrolled.
Multidrug Regimens: Stage 2 hypertension often requires a combination of two or more medications, sometimes available in a single daily pill.

Both ACE inhibitors and ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) are equally effective first-line treatments for high blood pressure, but ARBs are generally preferred for tolerability because they have a significantly lower risk of causing a persistent dry cough or angioedema.
Key Comparison
Mechanism Differences
ACE Inhibitors: Stop the enzyme that produces angiotensin II and inadvertently lead to a build-up of bradykinin, which triggers the characteristic dry cough and rare risk of swelling () in some people.
ARBs: Let angiotensin II be formed but prevent it from binding to its target receptors. Because they leave bradykinin alone, they spare patients the nagging cough.
Clinical Guidance & Selection
First-Line Status: Major guidelines (such as ACC/AHA and ESC/ESH) list ACE inhibitors, , thiazide diuretics, and calcium channel blockers (CCBs) as interchangeable first-line options.
Why ARBs are Gaining Ground: Recent clinical shifts lean toward starting with ARBs primarily because patients tolerate them much better, leading to higher long-term adherence.
When ACE Inhibitors Are Still Chosen: ACE inhibitors have a massive legacy of clinical trial data in specific settings (such as post-myocardial infarction or certain chronic kidney disease profiles), and cost or insurance formulary preferences sometimes make them the initial pick.
Crucial Rule: Never combine an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together, as dual blockade increases the risk of dangerously high potassium () and worsening kidney function without added clinical benefit.

Early Symptoms
In the early stages of PAH, you may not notice any symptoms at all. When initial signs do appear, they often develop slowly over months or years and are easy to confuse with other heart or lung conditions:

Fatigue and general tiredness.
Lightheadedness or dizziness, particularly when active.
Chest pain or pressure.
Heart palpitations (a racing or pounding heartbeat).
Advanced Symptoms
As the disease progresses and places more strain on the heart, symptoms can become more severe or occur even while resting:
Edema (swelling in the ankles, legs, feet, or lower abdomen/neck due to fluid retention).
Fainting spells (syncope) or severe dizziness during exertion.
Cyanosis (bluish or grayish tint to the lips, fingers, or skin from low oxygen levels).
Bloated abdomen or unexplained weight gain from fluid buildup.
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or hoarseness in rare, advanced cases where enlarged arteries press on chest nerves.

Early signs of type 2 diabetes develop slowly over months or years, and some people show no symptoms at all.
Common Early Warning Signs
Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar forces your kidneys to work harder to filter and absorb excess glucose, pulling fluid from your tissues and causing you to pee more often—especially at night.
Constant fatigue: Your cells cannot absorb glucose properly to use as fuel, leaving you feeling tired and weak.
Increased hunger: Because your body’s cells are starved of energy, you may feel hungry even after eating.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar can cause fluid to shift into the lenses of your eyes or damage retinal blood vessels, making your sight blurry.
Slow-healing cuts and sores: High blood sugar impairs circulation and your immune system, making it harder for wounds to heal.
Tingling or numbness: Known as peripheral neuropathy, high blood sugar can damage nerves, often causing a pins-and-needles sensation or numbness in the hands and feet.
Darkened skin patches: A condition called acanthosis nigricans causes dark, velvety patches of skin to form in folds and creases (such as the neck, armpits, or groin), which signals insulin resistance.
Frequent infections: Higher sugar levels in the blood and urine can feed bacteria and yeast, leading to recurrent urinary tract or skin infections.
Unexplained weight loss: Though less common in type 2 than type 1, your body may start burning fat and muscle for energy if it cannot use glucose.
You can learn more about risk factors and diagnostic blood tests through the Mayo Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Guide or the Cleveland Clinic Diabetes Overview.

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure your blood glucose or average blood sugar levels over time.
Key Diagnostic Blood Tests
Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) Test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months. Does not require fasting.
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: Measures your blood sugar after you do not eat or drink anything (except water) for at least 8 hours.
Two-Hour Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): Measures your blood sugar before and 2 hours after you drink a special high-sugar liquid (following an 8-hour fast).
Random Plasma Glucose Test: Measures your blood sugar at any time of day, regardless of when you last ate. Used if you have classic diabetes symptoms (such as extreme thirst or frequent urination).
Confirmation and Next Steps
Repeat Testing: Unless you have clear symptoms of high blood sugar combined with a high random reading, doctors usually repeat the test on a second day or use a second test to confirm the diagnosis.
Over-the-Counter Meters: Home fingerstick blood glucose meters cannot be used to officially diagnose diabetes; formal lab work is required.

Type 2 diabetes treatment options include a multi-step approach of lifestyle changes, oral or injectable medications, and sometimes insulin therapy or surgery to manage blood sugar levels.
1. Lifestyle Interventions
Diet: Follow a balanced eating plan focused on lean proteins, non-starchy vegetables, high-fiber foods, and healthy fats (such as the Mediterranean or DASH diet).
Physical Activity: Get regular exercise to help the body use insulin more effectively.
Weight Management: Achieving weight management significantly improves blood sugar control and insulin sensitivity.
2. Oral Medications (Pills)
Biguanides (Metformin): Usually the first medicine prescribed; it lowers glucose production in the liver and improves insulin sensitivity.
Sulfonylureas: (e.g., glipizide, glimepiride, glyburide) Stimulate the pancreas to produce more insulin.
TZDs (Thiazolidinediones): (e.g., pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) Help insulin work better in muscle and fat cells.
DPP-4 Inhibitors (Gliptins): (e.g., sitagliptin) Enhance incretin hormones to lower post-meal blood sugar.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: Help the kidneys remove excess glucose through the urine while offering heart and kidney protection.
Meglitinides & Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors: Stimulate fast insulin release around mealtimes or slow carbohydrate breakdown.
3. Non-Insulin Injectable Medications
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists & Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonists: (e.g., tirzepatide, semaglutide) Injectable drugs that lower blood sugar, support weight management, and reduce cardiovascular risks.
4. Insulin Therapy
Exogenous Insulin: Used if oral medications and lifestyle changes no longer keep blood sugar in target range, or if initial blood sugar/A1C levels are elevated. It can be long-acting, short-acting, or pre-mixed, delivered via pens, syringes, or pumps.
5. Surgical & Technological Options
Bariatric (Weight Loss) Surgery: Can help eligible individuals manage or achieve remission of type 2 diabetes.
Continuous Glucose Monitors (CGMs): Wearable sensors that track blood sugar trends in real time.

Jardiance (empagliflozin) can cause common side effects like increased urination, urinary tract infections (UTIs), and genital yeast infections, as well as serious risks such as diabetic ketoacidosis and dehydration.
Common Side Effects
Increased urination: Frequent or urgent need to pee as the medication clears excess sugar from your blood through your urine. Taking your dose in the morning can help reduce nighttime trips to the bathroom.
Urinary tract infections (UTIs): Burning, pain, urgency, or abnormal urine appearance.
Genital yeast infections: Fungal infections causing vaginal itching, burning, pain, or thick white discharge in women, and redness, irritation, or swelling around the penis or scrotum in men.
Increased thirst and weight loss: Mild fluid loss and metabolic changes can trigger extra thirst or modest changes in weight.
Serious Side Effects
Seek prompt medical attention or contact your healthcare provider if you notice signs of severe reactions:
Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): A life-threatening buildup of acid in the blood (which can happen even with normal blood sugar levels). Symptoms include fruity-smelling breath, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, extreme fatigue, and trouble breathing.
Dehydration and low blood pressure: Loss of water and salt can cause dizziness, lightheadedness, weakness, or fainting, especially when standing up. Risk is higher if you are over 65, have kidney issues, or take water pills (diuretics).
Severe kidney or urinary infections: Pyelonephritis or urosepsis, marked by high fever, chills, lower back or side pain, and bloody or cloudy urine.
Low blood sugar (Hypoglycemia): More likely if Jardiance is combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, causing shaking, sweating, fast heartbeat, or confusion.
Necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier's gangrene): A rare, severe, and life-threatening bacterial infection of the perineum (area between the genitals and anus) causing intense pain, swelling, and fever.
Lower limb amputations: An increased risk of toe or leg amputation has been observed, particularly in patients with pre-existing vascular disease or foot ulcers.
Serious allergic reactions: Swelling of the face, lips, or throat, hives, and difficulty breathing or swallowing.

High blood pressure (hypertension) is often called the "silent killer" because most people do not have any warning signs or symptoms, even if their numbers are high.
When Symptoms Do Appear
Symptoms rarely happen unless blood pressure rises to dangerous, life-threatening levels (such as a hypertensive crisis of 180/120 mm Hg or higher). In those cases, warning signs may include:
Severe headaches
Blurred vision or other vision changes
Shortness of breath
Chest pain or tightness
Dizziness or lightheadedness
Fatigue or confusion
Blood spots in the eyes
Nosebleeds (less common)
What to Do in an Emergency
According to the American Heart Association, if your blood pressure reading is 180/120 mm Hg or higher:
Wait one minute and take the reading again.
If it remains that high and you have symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, vision changes, or difficulty speaking, call 911 immediately.
If your reading is 180/120 mm Hg or higher without those symptoms, contact your doctor right away for guidance.
Blood Pressure Categories
The Mayo Clinic outlines standard blood pressure ranges:
Normal: Less than 120/80 mm Hg
Elevated: Systolic 120–129 and diastolic < 80
Stage 1 Hypertension: Systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89
Stage 2 Hypertension: Systolic 140+ or diastolic 90+

High blood pressure (hypertension) is diagnosed when your blood pressure readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.
Blood pressure is measured using two numbers: systolic (the top number, measuring pressure when the heart beats) and diastolic (the bottom number, measuring pressure when the heart rests between beats).
Blood Pressure Categories
According to guidelines from the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, blood pressure is grouped into the following ranges:
Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 1 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 130–139 mm Hg systolic or 80–89 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 2 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 140 mm Hg or higher systolic or 90 mm Hg or higher diastolic
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic
Urgent Warning Signs
Severe Hypertension (No Symptoms): If your reading is above 180/120 mm Hg but you feel fine, rest for a few minutes and recheck. If it remains that high, contact your healthcare professional immediately.
Hypertensive Emergency (With Symptoms): If your reading is above 180/120 mm Hg and you experience chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, a change in vision, or difficulty speaking, call 911 immediately.

Treatment options for hypertension (high blood pressure) combine heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications to lower blood pressure below the target goal of 130/80 mm Hg for most adults.
Lifestyle Modifications
Adopting healthy habits can lower blood pressure and reduce the number or dose of medications required:
DASH Eating Plan: Follow the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet, which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while reducing sodium.
Sodium Reduction: Limit daily salt intake (ideally aiming for under 1,500 to 2,000 mg per day).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as walking, cycling, or swimming.
Weight Management: Achieve and maintain a healthy body weight.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce or eliminate alcohol consumption and avoid tobacco products, which constrict blood vessels.
Quality Sleep: Aim for at least 7 hours of sleep per night and address conditions like sleep apnea.
First-Line Medications
When lifestyle changes are not enough, healthcare providers prescribe one or more American Heart Association first-line drug classes:
Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors: Keep blood vessels from narrowing (e.g., lisinopril, ramipril).
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Relax and widen blood vessels (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells to promote relaxation (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the body eliminate excess sodium and water, with thiazide diuretics most commonly prescribed (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide).
Additional and Combination Therapies
Beta-Blockers: Lower heart rate and cardiac output; often used if you have coexisting heart failure or coronary artery disease (metoprolol, carvedilol).
Multi-Drug and Fixed-Dose Combinations: More than 50% of people with hypertension require two or more medications, often taken as a single-pill combination to improve blood pressure control and adherence.
Resistant Hypertension: If blood pressure remains high despite taking three or more drugs (including a diuretic), providers may adjust dosages, check for secondary causes, or use specialized options like mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists or renal denervation.
Guidance and safety resources are also provided through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

ACE inhibitors (ACEis) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are both considered effective first-line treatments for high blood pressure, though ARBs are frequently favored as the initial choice due to a more favorable side effect profile—specifically a lower risk of chronic dry cough.
Efficacy and Blood Pressure Control
Equal effectiveness: Both drug classes lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure to a similar degree.
Cardiovascular and renal protection: Both provide comparable organ-protective benefits in patients with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or heart failure.
Large-scale analyses: Large population and network studies (such as the LEGEND-HTN analysis) suggest ARBs and ACEis perform similarly in preventing major cardiovascular events, with ARBs showing fewer treatment discontinuations.
Side Effects and Tolerability
Persistent dry cough: ACE inhibitors block the breakdown of bradykinin, which causes a dry, nagging cough in a notable minority of patients (often leading to a switch). ARBs do not affect bradykinin and rarely cause this cough.
Angioedema: Both classes carry a small risk of angioedema (swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat), though it is significantly more common with ACE inhibitors.
High potassium and kidney function: Both classes can elevate serum potassium (hyperkalemia) and cause mild, reversible changes in creatinine/renal function, requiring periodic bloodwork monitoring.
Combination warning: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be prescribed together, as dual blockade increases the risk of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury without improving cardiovascular outcomes.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which forces the right side of the heart to work harder.
Early Symptoms
In the early stages, PAH often causes no noticeable symptoms. When signs do appear, they frequently mimic other heart or lung conditions:
Shortness of breath (dyspnea) during everyday activities like walking or climbing stairs
Fatigue and general weakness
Chest pressure or pain
Heart palpitations or a racing, pounding heartbeat
Advanced Symptoms
As the condition progresses and the right side of the heart begins to strain or fail, more severe symptoms develop:
Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting (syncope), especially during physical exertion
Swelling (edema) in the ankles, legs, feet, or abdomen
Bluish or gray lips and skin (cyanosis)
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) in rare or advanced cases
Voice hoarseness caused by an enlarged pulmonary artery pressing on a nerve

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over years, and many people have no obvious symptoms in the early stages.
Common Early Warning Signs
Frequent urination: Needing to go to the bathroom more often, especially at night, as your kidneys try to flush out extra sugar.
Excessive thirst: Feeling constantly thirsty because frequent urination leads to mild dehydration.
Persistent fatigue: Feeling unusually tired or drained because your cells cannot effectively absorb glucose for energy.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar causing fluid shifts that swell the lenses of your eyes.
Slow-healing wounds: Minor cuts, bruises, or sores taking a long time to heal due to poor circulation and immune function.
Tingling or numbness: A "pins and needles" sensation, burning, or pain in the hands or feet from early nerve irritation (neuropathy).
Unexplained weight changes: Losing weight without trying because the body cannot absorb glucose properly, or sometimes gaining weight linked to insulin resistance.
Increased hunger: Feeling hungry (polyphagia) even after eating because energy isn't reaching your cells.
Darkened skin patches: Developing velvety, dark patches of skin (acanthosis nigricans) around the neck, armpits, or groin, which indicate insulin resistance.
Frequent infections: Experiencing repeat urinary tract infections (UTIs), yeast infections, or skin issues because bacteria and fungi thrive on high sugar levels.
How to Get Screened
Because symptoms can be subtle or absent, doctors diagnose Type 2 diabetes using simple blood tests:
A1C test: Measures average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months (6.5% or higher indicates diabetes).
Fasting plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar after an 8-hour fast (126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes).
Random plasma glucose test: Checked at any time without fasting (200 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes).

Blood pressure is considered high (hypertension) when it reaches or exceeds 130/80 mm Hg, according to the guidelines from the American Heart Association.
Blood Pressure Categories
Readings are measured using two numbers: systolic (top number, the pressure when your heart beats) and diastolic (bottom number, the pressure when your heart rests between beats).
Normal: Less than 120/80 mm Hg
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg (systolic) and less than 80 mm Hg (diastolic)
Stage 1 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 130–139 mm Hg (systolic) OR 80–89 mm Hg (diastolic)
Stage 2 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 140 mm Hg or higher (systolic) OR 90 mm Hg or higher (diastolic)
Hypertensive Crisis / Severe Hypertension: Higher than 180 mm Hg (systolic) AND/OR higher than 120 mm Hg (diastolic)
What to Do for High Readings
Stage 1 or Stage 2: Schedule a visit with your health care provider to discuss lifestyle changes and potential medication.
Hypertensive Crisis (>180/120 mm Hg): Wait 5 minutes and retest. If your reading remains this high and you experience symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, backache, numbness, or vision changes, call 911 immediately.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is treated through a combination of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when needed, prescription medications. The primary goal for most adults is to reach a blood pressure level of less than 130/80 mm Hg.
1. Lifestyle Modifications
Lifestyle changes are recommended for everyone with high blood pressure and can sometimes reduce or delay the need for medication:
DASH Eating Plan: Focus on a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fats.
Sodium Reduction: Lower salt intake (aiming for less than 2,000 mg or around 1,500 mg per day) to help drop blood pressure.
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise (such as brisk walking) and resistance training.
Weight Management: Lose weight or maintain a healthy weight if you are overweight or obese.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce alcohol consumption and stop smoking or using tobacco products to protect your blood vessels.
Better Sleep: Aim for at least seven hours of quality sleep per night and screen for conditions like sleep apnea.
2. First-Line Medications
When lifestyle changes alone are not enough, doctors prescribe blood pressure-lowering drugs. Treatment often starts with a single medication or a combination of two drugs (sometimes in a single pill):
ACE Inhibitors (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors): Relax and widen blood vessels (e.g., lisinopril).
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): Block the action of chemicals that narrow blood vessels (e.g., losartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells to let vessels relax (e.g., amlodipine).
Thiazide Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the body get rid of extra sodium and water.
(Note: For Black patients, guidelines often recommend thiazide diuretics or calcium channel blockers as preferred first-line choices).
3. Additional or Specialized Options
If blood pressure remains uncontrolled (resistant hypertension) or if you have specific heart, kidney, or metabolic conditions, other classes of medications may be added:
Beta-Blockers: Lower heart rate and heart workload (often used if you have coronary artery disease or heart failure).
Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists (MRAs): Block aldosterone to reduce fluid and salt retention (such as spironolactone).
Central-Acting Agents or Vasodilators: Less common or specialized options for hard-to-treat blood pressure.
Newer Interventions: For stubborn or resistant cases, procedures like renal denervation (which targets kidney nerve activity) or the addition of GLP-1 medications (for patients with obesity/diabetes) may be evaluated by a specialist.

ACE inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs) are both recognized as equal first-line options for treating high blood pressure by major medical guidelines, though large comparative studies show they have identical cardiovascular effectiveness with a more favorable safety profile for ARBs.
Effectiveness
Cardiovascular Protection: Head-to-head research (such as large cohort analyses published in Hypertension and ) shows no significant difference between ACE inhibitors and ARBs in preventing heart attacks, strokes, heart failure hospitalizations, or composite cardiac events.
Blood Pressure Control: Both drug classes lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure effectively through the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS).
Side Effects and Safety Profile
Dry Cough: ACE inhibitors frequently cause a persistent, dry, nagging cough (affecting roughly 1% to 10% of patients) because of bradykinin buildup. ARBs block angiotensin receptors without affecting bradykinin, leading to a significantly lower risk of cough.
Angioedema: ACE inhibitors carry a higher risk of angioedema (swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or airway), which is rare but potentially dangerous. ARBs have a substantially lower risk of this reaction.
Other Risks: Studies also link ACE inhibitors to a higher relative risk of side effects like acute pancreatitis compared to ARBs.
Shared Precautions & Contraindications
Pregnancy: Neither class should be used during pregnancy due to the risk of severe fetal harm or birth defects.
Combination Therapy: ACE inhibitors and ARBs must not be combined together, as dual RAAS blockade dramatically increases the risk of dangerous hyperkalemia (high blood potassium) and kidney injury without added cardiovascular benefit.
Kidney Function: Both require monitoring of serum creatinine and potassium levels, and they should be used with caution or avoided in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) occurs when the tiny arteries in your lungs thicken, narrow, or block. This makes it hard for blood to flow and forces the right side of your heart to work much harder.

Advanced or Progressive Symptoms
Swelling (edema): Fluid buildup causing swollen ankles, legs, or a bloated abdomen (as blood backs up into the liver and kidneys).
Bluish or gray lips and skin (cyanosis): A sign of low oxygen levels in the blood.

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over many years, and early symptoms can be very mild or completely absent.
Common Early Warning Signs
Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar forces your kidneys to work overtime to flush out the excess sugar, which pulls water from your tissues and makes you feel constantly thirsty.
Persistent fatigue: When your cells cannot properly absorb glucose for energy, you may feel unusually tired or exhausted even after getting enough rest.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar can cause temporary fluid shifts or swelling in the lens of the eyes.
Slow-healing sores or cuts: Elevated blood sugar impairs circulation and weakens the immune response, making minor wounds take much longer to heal.
Tingling or numbness: Peripheral nerve damage (neuropathy) can start as a mild tingling, burning, or loss of sensation in the hands or feet.
Frequent infections: Bacteria and fungi thrive on excess sugar, leading to recurring urinary tract infections (UTIs), yeast infections, or skin issues.
Unexplained weight changes: You may experience unexpected weight loss (as the body starts burning fat and muscle for energy) or gradual weight gain tied to insulin resistance.
Darkened skin patches: A condition called acanthosis nigricans causes velvety, dark patches of skin to form around the neck, armpits, or groin, signaling underlying insulin resistance.

Type 2 diabetes treatment options center on lifestyle changes, oral or injectable medications, and surgical or monitoring approaches.
1. Lifestyle Modifications
Dietary Changes: Focus on whole foods, non-starchy vegetables, lean proteins, and complex carbohydrates while managing overall calorie intake. Weight management approaches can help improve insulin sensitivity.

Metformin: Typically prescribed as a first-line oral medication; it reduces glucose production in the liver and improves insulin sensitivity.

Insulin Therapy: Used when other treatments no longer keep blood sugar in range or when natural insulin production declines significantly; available in long-acting, short-acting, or pre-mixed forms via pens, syringes, or pumps.

Weight-Loss (Bariatric) Surgery: Can be an option for adults with a higher BMI or co-existing conditions to help manage or put type 2 diabetes into remission.

Jardiance (empagliflozin) is a prescription medication that works by helping your kidneys remove extra sugar through your urine. Because of how it changes fluid and sugar balance, it can cause several common and serious side effects.
You can review complete safety details through the Jardiance Official Safety Guide.
Common Side Effects
Increased Urination: Needing to pee more often or in larger amounts as the body flushes out excess glucose.
Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs): Symptoms include a burning sensation during urination, frequent urgency, cloudy or bloody urine, and lower back or pelvic pain.
Genital Yeast Infections: More common in women (vaginal itching, burning, and thick white discharge), though men can also develop yeast infections around the penis or scrotum.
Dehydration and Dizziness: Feeling lightheaded, dizzy, or weak—especially when standing up—due to fluid and salt loss.

Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): A dangerous buildup of acid in the blood that can happen even if blood sugar levels are not very high. Warning signs include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, unusual fatigue, trouble breathing, and a fruity odor on your breath.
Necrotizing Fasciitis (Fournier's Gangrene): A rare but life-threatening bacterial infection of the tissue under the skin in the perineum (area between the genitals and the anus) causing severe pain, swelling, redness, and fever.
Severe Kidney Injury or Infections: Sudden worsening of kidney function or serious kidney infections (pyelonephritis).
Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia): More likely if Jardiance is taken alongside other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas.
Lower Limb Amputations: An increased risk reported with SGLT2 inhibitors, particularly for people with a history of prior amputations, foot ulcers, or severe peripheral vascular disease.
Serious Allergic Reactions: Hives or swelling of the face, lips, tongue, and throat causing difficulty swallowing or breathing.

Neither SGLT2 inhibitors nor GLP-1 receptor agonists have completely replaced metformin as the universal first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes, though guidelines from groups like the American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommend them as direct first-line or early add-on options for patients with specific cardiorenal risks.
Choosing between an SGLT2 inhibitor and a GLP-1 receptor agonist depends heavily on individual patient organ protection needs and side effect profiles:
SGLT2 Inhibitors (Oral)
Primary Strengths: Superior for heart failure (reducing hospitalizations and cardiac outcomes) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) (slowing progression of renal decline).
Formulation: Mostly taken as a daily pill (oral).
Other Benefits: Moderate weight loss and blood pressure reduction.
Key Risks/Considerations: Risk of genital fungal infections, urinary tract infections, volume depletion, and rare diabetic ketoacidosis; less potent for lowering HbA1c than GLP-1s.
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (Mostly Injectable)
Primary Strengths: Superior for HbA1c/blood sugar lowering, weight loss , and stroke prevention (ASCVD). Oral semaglutide (Rybelsus) is a pill option, though most are weekly injections.
Formulation: Mostly weekly subcutaneous injections, with oral options available.
Other Benefits: Significant cardiovascular risk reduction and emerging renal benefits.
Key Risks/Considerations: Gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) and a contraindication for individuals with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2).
Head-to-Head Comparison & Combination Therapy
MACE/Cardiovascular Outcomes: Major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) reduction is comparable between both classes.
Combination Therapy: If cost and insurance allow, using both agents together provides complementary benefits for glycemic control, weight, heart, and kidney health.

High blood pressure (hypertension) is often called a "silent killer" because most people do not have any symptoms. You can live with high blood pressure for years without feeling sick or noticing anything is wrong.
Symptoms During Dangerously High Blood Pressure (Hypertensive Crisis)
Symptoms usually only appear if your blood pressure rises to extreme levels (typically above 180/120 mm Hg). These signs may include:
Severe headaches
Shortness of breath
Chest pain
Dizziness or lightheadedness
Vision changes (such as blurred or double vision)
Sudden confusion, numbness, or weakness (which can signal a stroke)
Blood spots in the eyes
Nosebleeds
Less Specific or Subtle Signs
Some people with chronically high blood pressure may experience subtle or easy-to-dismiss signs, such as:
Constant fatigue or exhaustion
Pounding sensations in the chest, neck, or ears
What to Do in an Emergency
According to the American Heart Association:
If your blood pressure reading is above 180/120 mm Hg, wait one minute and recheck it.
If it remains that high and you have emergency symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, vision changes, weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking, call 911 immediately.
If your reading is above 180/120 mm Hg but you feel fine, contact your healthcare provider right away.
How to Know Your Numbers
Because symptoms are rare, the only reliable way to check for high blood pressure is through regular readings at a doctor's office or with an approved home monitor, as outlined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Blood pressure is considered high when it is consistently 130/80 mm Hg or higher, according to guidelines from the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Blood pressure readings use two numbers:
Systolic (top number): Measures pressure in your arteries when your heart beats.
Diastolic (bottom number): Measures pressure in your arteries when your heart rests between beats.
Blood Pressure Categories
Normal: Less than 120/80 mm Hg
Elevated: Systolic between 120–129 and diastolic less than 80 mm Hg
Stage 1 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89 mm Hg
Stage 2 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Systolic 140 or higher or diastolic 90 or higher mm Hg
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Systolic higher than 180 and/or diastolic higher than 120 mm Hg

Treatment options for high blood pressure (hypertension) include lifestyle changes, prescription medications, and medical procedures.
Lifestyle Modifications
Adopting a heart-healthy routine is the first step or a helpful companion to medication:
DASH Eating Plan: Focus on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fat and cholesterol.
Reduce Sodium: Limit salt intake to under 2,000 mg (or ideally under 1,500 mg) per day.
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as walking, swimming, or biking, for at least 2.5 hours per week.
Weight Management: Lose excess weight if you have overweight or obesity.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce alcohol consumption and stop smoking or using tobacco products.
Improve Sleep: Aim for at least 7 hours of quality sleep per night.
Prescription Medications
When lifestyle changes alone do not lower blood pressure below the target goal (typically under 130/80 mm Hg for most adults), doctors prescribe medications:
ACE Inhibitors & ARBs: Relax and widen blood vessels (e.g., lisinopril, losartan).
Calcium Channel Blocker (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering muscle cells in the heart and blood vessels to keep them relaxed (e.g., amlodipine).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the body remove excess sodium and water (e.g., thiazide diuretics like hydrochlorothiazide).
Other Options: Beta-blockers, alpha-blockers, central-acting agents, or vasodilators may be added depending on other health conditions like heart failure or kidney disease. Many patients need a combination of two or more drugs, sometimes combined into a single pill.
You can read more detailed drug classes through the American Heart Association.
Procedural Options
Renal Denervation: A minimally invasive, FDA-approved procedure that targets nerves in the arteries leading to the kidneys to help lower blood pressure in patients with uncontrolled or resistant hypertension.

Jardiance (empagliflozin) can cause a range of common and serious side effects because it works by helping your kidneys remove excess sugar through your urine.
Common Side Effects
Urinary tract infections (UTIs): Symptoms include burning, urgency, frequency, and cloudy or bloody urine.
Genital yeast infections: These can affect both women (itching, burning, thick white discharge) and men (redness, itching, swelling, or pain around the penis).
Increased urination: You may need to pee more often or in larger amounts than usual.
Other mild effects: Upper respiratory tract infections, increased thirst, nausea, joint pain, and mild weight loss.
Serious Side Effects (Seek Medical Attention)
Dehydration and low blood pressure: Loss of water and salt can cause dizziness, lightheadedness, or feeling faint—especially when standing up.
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): A life-threatening buildup of acid in the blood, which can happen even if your blood sugar is not very high. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, tiredness, trouble breathing, and fruity-smelling breath.
Severe urinary tract or kidney infections: Such as pyelonephritis or urosepsis, marked by high fever, chills, and lower back or side pain.
Necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier's gangrene): A rare but life-threatening bacterial infection of the tissue under the skin in the perineum (area between the genitals and anus) causing severe pain, redness, and swelling.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): More likely if you take Jardiance alongside other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas.
Lower limb amputations: An increased risk has been observed, particularly in patients with a history of amputation, peripheral vascular disease, or foot ulcers.
Severe allergic reactions: Symptoms include hives and swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, leading to trouble swallowing or breathing.

Modern guidelines from organizations like the American Diabetes Association no longer treat older medications as a strict one-size-fits-all starting point for type 2 diabetes. When to Prioritize Each Class
Choose an SGLT2 Inhibitor if: The patient has a history of heart failure (especially with reduced ejection fraction) or chronic kidney disease, or prefers a daily pill over injections.
Choose a GLP-1 Receptor Agonist if: The patient needs strong glycemic control, substantial weight loss, or has a high risk of stroke or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and is comfortable with weekly injections.
Combination Therapy: In many high-risk patients, doctors combine both classes because they work through different mechanisms and provide complementary heart, kidney, and metabolic protection.

High blood pressure (hypertension) usually causes no symptoms at all, which is why it is often called the "silent killer". Many people can live with high blood pressure for years without realizing it while it slowly damages the heart, brain, and kidneys.

Shortness of breath
Chest pain
Vision changes (such as blurred vision)
Nosebleeds

Fatigue or exhaustion

Chest pain
Shortness of breath
Back pain
Numbness or weakness
Change in vision
Difficulty speaking or confusion

High blood pressure (hypertension) is officially diagnosed when your blood pressure readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.
Blood pressure is measured using two numbers: systolic (the top number, measuring pressure when the heart beats) and diastolic (the bottom number, measuring pressure when the heart rests between beats).
Blood Pressure Categories
Blood pressure ranges from the American Heart Association and CDC are categorized as follows:
Normal: Less than 120/80 mm Hg
Elevated: 120–129 systolic and less than 80 diastolic
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130–139 systolic or 80–89 diastolic
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140+ systolic or 90+ diastolic
Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 systolic and/or higher than 120 diastolic
What to Do If Your Numbers Are High
Stage 1 or 2: Consult a doctor, as a single reading isn't a definitive diagnosis. Providers evaluate patterns over time or home monitoring.
Above 180/120 mm Hg: Retest after five minutes. If readings remain high with symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, or weakness, call 911. Without symptoms, contact your doctor immediately.

Treatment options for high blood pressure (hypertension) include lifestyle changes, prescription medications, and medical procedures. The standard blood pressure treatment goal for most adults is less than 130/80 mm Hg.
Lifestyle Modifications
Adopting heart-healthy habits can lower blood pressure or reduce the number of medications needed:
DASH Eating Plan: Focus on a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on sodium (salt).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming.
Weight Management: Achieve and maintain a healthy body weight.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce or eliminate alcohol consumption and stop using tobacco products, which constrict blood vessels.
Quality Sleep: Aim for at least seven hours of sleep per night and manage daily stress.
Prescription Medications
When lifestyle changes are not enough—or immediately upon diagnosis if you have high cardiovascular risk, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease—doctors may prescribe one or more drugs. The primary classes of blood pressure medications include:
ACE Inhibitors (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors): Relax blood vessels to improve blood flow (e.g., lisinopril, ramipril).
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): Block the action of chemicals that narrow blood vessels (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells, allowing vessels to relax (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the kidneys remove excess sodium and water from the body, lowering fluid volume (e.g., thiazides like hydrochlorothiazide).
Beta-Blockers: Lower heart rate and reduce the force of heart contractions (e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol) — often used if you have co-existing heart conditions.
Note: More than half of people with hypertension require two or more medications combined—sometimes in a single pill—to reach their target goal.
Procedural Options
Renal Denervation: A minimally invasive, FDA-approved procedure that targets nerves in the renal arteries to help lower blood pressure in patients with uncontrolled or resistant hypertension.
You can read more about medical classes through the American Heart Association or guidelines via the National Institutes of Health.

Losartan is a prescription medication used to treat high blood pressure, protect kidney function in people with type 2 diabetes, and lower the risk of stroke. While generally well tolerated, it can cause several side effects.
Common Side Effects
Dizziness or Lightheadedness: Most likely to happen when you first start losartan or after a dose increase, especially when standing up quickly (orthostatic hypotension).
Fatigue and Weakness: Feeling tired as your body adjusts to a lower blood pressure.
Cold-like Symptoms: Stuffy or runny nose, sore throat, or upper respiratory tract infections.
Digestive Upset: Nausea, diarrhea, or mild stomach pain.
Back or Joint Pain: Aches in your back, muscles, or joints.
Headache: Mild tension headaches, which often fade after a week or two.
Serious Side Effects (Seek Medical Attention)
Angioedema (Severe Allergic Reaction): Sudden swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing. (This is a medical emergency.)
High Potassium Levels (Hyperkalemia): Muscle weakness, confusion, numbness or tingling, or a slow, fast, or irregular heartbeat.
Kidney Problems: Unexplained swelling in your hands, ankles, or feet, or a big change in how much urine you pass.
Severely Low Blood Pressure: Fainting, severe dizziness, or extreme lightheadedness.
Liver Issues: Yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice) or severe upper stomach pain.
Important Safety Notes
Do not stop taking losartan on your own, even if you experience mild side effects. Stopping suddenly can cause your blood pressure to spike.
Pregnancy Warning: Losartan should not be taken during pregnancy because it can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby (especially in the second and third trimesters).

Both ACE inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors) and ARBs (angiotensin II receptor blockers) are equally recommended as first-line therapies for high blood pressure in major clinical guidelines .
Key Similarities
Efficacy: Both lower blood pressure effectively by targeting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) to relax and widen blood vessels.
Organ Protection: Both provide kidney and heart protective benefits, making them preferred choices for patients with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or heart failure.
Rule: You should take either an ACE inhibitor or an ARB, never both at the same time, as combining them increases the risk of kidney dysfunction and high potassium without added benefit .
Key Differences
Mechanism of Action: ACE inhibitors stop the body from producing angiotensin II (an enzyme blocker, ending in -pril like lisinopril). ARBs block angiotensin II from binding to its receptors (receptor blocker, ending in -sartan like losartan).
Side Effects (The Main Differentiator): ACE inhibitors frequently cause a persistent, dry, nagging cough in a notable minority of patients. ARBs do not cause this cough.
Preference Trends: Because of the lower rate of side effects (specifically the lack of cough), recent clinical analyses and studies increasingly lean toward preferentially prescribing ARBs over ACE inhibitors as an initial first-line choice.
Safety Warning: Both classes are strictly contraindicated during pregnancy due to the risk of severe fetal harm.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, making the right side of the heart work harder.
Early and Common Symptoms
In the early stages, PAH may cause no symptoms. As the condition progresses, signs often mimic other heart and lung diseases:
Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially during physical activity or exertion (such as climbing stairs or walking)
Fatigue and general tiredness
Chest pain or pressure
Dizziness or lightheadedness
Heart palpitations (a racing or pounding heartbeat)
Advanced Symptoms
As the right side of the heart faces increasing strain and begins to weaken, more severe symptoms can develop:
Fainting or syncopal spells (especially during or after exertion)
Swelling (edema) in the ankles, legs, or feet
Swollen abdomen (ascites) caused by fluid retention
Bluish color on the lips and skin (cyanosis)
Hoarseness from enlarged pulmonary arteries pressing on nearby nerves

Opsumit (macitentan) is an oral medication used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Like all prescription drugs, it can cause both common and serious side effects.
Common Side Effects
The most frequent side effects reported in clinical studies include:
Headache (about 14% of patients)
Nasopharyngitis (common cold symptoms or stuffy/runny nose)
Bronchitis or upper respiratory tract infections
Anemia (low red blood cell count, usually occurring during the first weeks of treatment)
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) and influenza (flu-like symptoms)
Peripheral edema (swelling in the hands, lower legs, or feet)
Serious Side Effects and Warnings
Serious Birth Defects: Opsumit can cause severe harm or death to an unborn baby. It is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy, and females who can become pregnant must have a negative pregnancy test before starting treatment, take regular tests, and use reliable contraception.
Liver Damage (Hepatotoxicity): Opsumit can affect liver function. Doctors typically check liver enzymes before starting treatment and monitor them periodically. Seek medical help right away if you notice signs of liver problems, such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe right-sided upper stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or unusual fatigue.
Fluid Retention: Excess fluid buildup or worsening swelling can happen, particularly during the first few weeks of therapy. Notify your doctor if you experience rapid weight gain or trouble breathing.
Decreased Sperm Counts: Opsumit may reduce sperm counts and impact male fertility.

Type 2 diabetes develops slowly, and many people have mild or no symptoms in the early stages.
When early signs appear, they are usually subtle and include:
Common Early Signs
Frequent urination: Needing to go to the bathroom more often, especially at night, as your kidneys try to flush out extra sugar.
Increased thirst: Feeling unusually thirsty or dry-mouthed because frequent urination leads to mild dehydration.
Persistent fatigue: Feeling very tired or drained because your cells cannot properly absorb glucose (sugar) for energy.
Constant hunger: Feeling hungry even after eating, because your body fails to convert blood sugar into cellular fuel.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar pulling fluid from the lenses of your eyes, making it hard to focus.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: Minor bruises, cuts, or blisters taking much longer to heal due to poor circulation and high blood sugar.
Tingling or numbness: A "pins and needles" sensation or loss of feeling in your hands or feet, which is an early sign of nerve irritation (neuropathy).
Frequent infections: More frequent urinary tract infections (UTIs), yeast infections, or skin issues, since bacteria and fungi thrive on extra sugar.
Darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin typically appearing around the neck, armpits, or groin, which can signal insulin resistance.
How Type 2 Diabetes Is Diagnosed
Because symptoms can be easy to miss, doctors rely on simple blood tests to catch the condition early or identify prediabetes:
Fasting plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar after an 8-hour fast; 126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.
A1C test: Shows your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months; 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes.
Random plasma glucose test: Checked at any time of day; 200 mg/dL or higher (with symptoms) indicates diabetes.
You can learn more about symptoms and diagnostic guidelines through the Mayo Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Guide.

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure your blood sugar levels or average blood glucose over time . Doctors usually require the test results to be confirmed on a second day unless clear symptoms are present.
Key Diagnostic Blood Tests
Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) Test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months.
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: Measures your blood sugar after you have not eaten or drank anything except water for at least 8 hours.
2-Hour Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): Measures your blood sugar before and 2 hours after you drink a special sugary liquid.
Random Plasma Glucose Test: Measures your blood sugar at any time of day, regardless of when you last ate, paired with classic diabetes symptoms (such as extreme thirst, frequent urination, or unexplained weight loss).
Confirmation and Distinction
Repeat Testing: Except in cases with severe, classic symptoms and a high random blood sugar reading, doctors typically repeat the diagnostic test on a different day to confirm the results.
Distinguishing Type 2 from Type 1: Because type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes are treated differently, your doctor may occasionally order additional bloodwork—such as checking for autoantibodies or C-peptide levels—if it is unclear which type you have.
