Type 2 diabetes treatment focuses on lowering blood sugar, managing weight, and preventing organ or heart damage. Doctors use a step-by-step approach that combines healthy habits, oral or injectable medications, and sometimes surgery.
1. Lifestyle Changes (The Foundation)
Healthy Eating: Choose non-starchy vegetables, lean proteins, and complex carbohydrates while cutting back on added sugars and refined grains.
Physical Activity: Incorporating regular moderate-to-vigorous exercise (such as brisk walking) plus muscle-strengthening sessions supports overall metabolic health.
Weight Management: Losing a modest percentage of your body weight can improve how your body uses insulin and help lower blood pressure and cholesterol.
2. Oral Medications (Pills)
If diet and exercise are not enough, doctors usually prescribe pills first. Many people take a combination of these drugs:
Metformin (Biguanide): This is almost always the first-line medication. It lowers how much glucose your liver makes and helps your cells respond better to insulin.
Sulfonylureas: Medications like glipizide and glimepiride make the pancreas release more insulin.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: These pills help your kidneys remove extra sugar through your urine, and they can also protect your heart and kidneys.
DPP-4 Inhibitors (Gliptins): These help block digestive enzymes to keep blood sugar from spiking after meals.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): Drugs like pioglitazone make muscle and fat cells more sensitive to insulin.
Meglitinides: Fast-acting pills taken around meal times to trigger a quick release of insulin.
3. Injectable Medications (Non-Insulin)
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: Injectable drugs (such as semaglutide or liraglutide) slow down digestion, help you feel full, encourage your pancreas to release insulin when needed, and often assist with weight loss.
Dual GLP-1/GIP Agonists: Newer combination injectables that provide even stronger blood sugar and weight management.
4. Insulin Therapy
If your pancreas eventually produces very little insulin, or if other medications do not keep your numbers in range, your doctor may prescribe insulin injections (long-acting, short-acting, or a mix) or an insulin pump.
5. Surgical & Procedural Options
Weight Loss (Bariatric) Surgery: Recommended for individuals with severe obesity, this surgery can dramatically improve blood sugar control and sometimes put type 2 diabetes into remission.

Common and serious side effects of Jardiance (empagliflozin) range from mild, manageable conditions to rare, life-threatening complications.
Common Side Effects
Urinary tract infections (UTIs): Symptoms include a burning sensation when urinating, frequent urgency, or cloudy/bloody urine.

Neither class is universally prescribed over the other as a standalone first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes. While traditional guidelines long mandated metformin as the primary first-line agent, modern American Diabetes Association (ADA) and European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) guidelines recommend choosing SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) or GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) as first-line or early options based on specific patient comorbidities (such as atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease) rather than a rigid glucose-lowering hierarchy.
Key Clinical Differences
How to Choose Between Them
Choose an SGLT2 Inhibitor first if: The patient has predominant heart failure (with reduced ejection fraction) or chronic kidney disease (CKD), or prefers a daily oral pill.
Choose a GLP-1 Receptor Agonist first if: The patient has established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), high stroke risk, significant obesity requiring substantial weight loss, or needs stronger HbA1c lowering.
Combination Therapy: Guidelines note that using both classes together provides synergistic cardiorenal, glycemic, and weight-loss benefits when cost and tolerability allow.

High blood pressure (hypertension) is officially diagnosed when your readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.

Normal: Less than 120 / less than 80 mm Hg
Elevated: 120–129 / less than 80 mm Hg

Treatment for high blood pressure (hypertension) combines heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when needed, prescription medications.
1. Lifestyle Modifications
Lifestyle changes are recommended for everyone with elevated blood pressure or hypertension, and can sometimes reduce or delay the need for medication:
DASH Eating Plan: Follow a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products, while cutting back on saturated fat and cholesterol (such as the NHLBI DASH Eating Plan).
Reduce Sodium: Lower daily salt and sodium intake (aiming for less than 2,000 mg or lower per day).
Regular Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise (like brisk walking, cycling, or swimming).
Weight Management: Lose extra weight if overweight or obese to ease the workload on your heart.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Avoid heavy alcohol use and stop smoking cigarettes or using tobacco, which immediately narrows blood vessels.
Improve Sleep: Aim for at least 7 hours of quality sleep per night.
2. First-Line Medications
When lifestyle changes are not enough—or immediately upon diagnosis if your blood pressure is very high or you have high cardiovascular risk, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease—your doctor may prescribe medication. Common first-line classes include:
ACE Inhibitors (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme inhibitors): e.g., lisinopril, ramipril; they keep blood vessels from narrowing.
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): e.g., losartan, valsartan; they block the effects of chemicals that narrow blood vessels.
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem; they relax and widen blood vessels by preventing calcium from entering muscle cells.
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): e.g., thiazides like hydrochlorothiazide or chlorthalidone; they help the body flush out excess sodium and water.
3. Additional or Specialized Medications
If blood pressure remains uncontrolled (resistant hypertension) or if you have specific heart or kidney conditions, your doctor may add other classes:
Beta-Blockers: e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol; often used if you have a history of heart attack, heart failure, or fast heart rate.
Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists / Spironolactone: Blocks aldosterone to help remove extra fluid.
Central-Acting Agents or Vasodilators: e.g., clonidine or hydralazine, used in specific multi-drug regimens.
Many people require a combination of two or more blood pressure drugs—often available in a single daily pill—to reach their target blood pressure (typically less than 130/80 mm Hg for most adults). Both ACE inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors) and ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) are recognized as effective first-line treatments for essential hypertension.
How They Work
ACE Inhibitors: Block the enzyme that produces angiotensin II, a substance that narrows blood vessels. Examples include lisinopril, ramipril, and enalapril.
ARBs: Block the specific receptors that angiotensin II binds to, preventing blood vessel constriction. Examples include losartan and valsartan.
Key Differences as First-Line Options
Efficacy: Both classes are equally effective at lowering systolic blood pressure (SBP), with ACE inhibitors offering a minor or comparable effect on diastolic blood pressure (DBP).
Side Effects (Cough): ACE inhibitors frequently cause a persistent, dry, nagging cough in a minority of patients due to the buildup of bradykinin. ARBs do not block bradykinin breakdown in the same way, making a dry cough rare.
Tolerability: Because of the lower rate of side effects like cough, ARBs are often preferred or chosen over ACE inhibitors when starting new therapy. If a patient cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor, an ARB is a standard direct substitute.
Combination Warning: Do not combine an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together. Using both simultaneously does not provide better outcomes and significantly increases the risk of side effects like high potassium (hyperkalemia) and kidney dysfunction .

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which strains the right side of the heart.
Early and Common Symptoms
Shortness of breath (dyspnea): Often starts during physical exertion, such as walking or climbing stairs, and worsens over time.
Fatigue and weakness: Persistent tiredness caused by the heart struggling to pump enough oxygen-rich blood through the body.
Chest pain or pressure: Can occur during exertion or rest due to the overworked heart muscle.
Palpitations or fast pulse: A rapid, pounding, or irregular heartbeat as the heart tries to keep up with demand.
Dizziness or lightheadedness: Especially during physical activity.
Advanced or Progressing Symptoms
Swelling (edema): Fluid buildup causing swollen ankles, legs, or a bloated abdomen as blood backs up toward the liver and heart.
Fainting (syncope): Occurs when the heart cannot supply enough blood flow to the brain, frequently triggered by exertion.
Bluish lips or skin (cyanosis): A sign of low oxygen levels in the blood.
Because early symptoms resemble asthma or other common lung and heart conditions, PAH can be difficult to catch right away. To learn more about diagnostic tests like echocardiograms or find patient resources, visit the American Lung Association Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Guide or consult the Mayo Clinic Pulmonary Hypertension Overview.

Opsumit (macitentan) is an oral medication used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Like all prescription drugs, it can cause both common and serious side effects.
Common Side Effects
The most frequent side effects reported in clinical studies include:
Headache (about 14% of patients)
Nasopharyngitis (common cold symptoms or stuffy/runny nose)
Bronchitis or upper respiratory tract infections
Anemia (low red blood cell count, usually occurring during the first weeks of treatment)
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) and influenza (flu-like symptoms)
Peripheral edema (swelling in the hands, lower legs, or feet)
Serious Side Effects and Warnings
Serious Birth Defects: Opsumit can cause severe harm or death to an unborn baby. It is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy, and females who can become pregnant must have a negative pregnancy test before starting treatment, take regular tests, and use reliable contraception.
Liver Damage (Hepatotoxicity): Opsumit can affect liver function. Doctors typically check liver enzymes before starting treatment and monitor them periodically. Seek medical help right away if you notice signs of liver problems, such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe right-sided upper stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or unusual fatigue.
Fluid Retention: Excess fluid buildup or worsening swelling can happen, particularly during the first few weeks of therapy. Notify your doctor if you experience rapid weight gain or trouble breathing.
Decreased Sperm Counts: Opsumit may reduce sperm counts and impact male fertility.

Type 2 diabetes develops slowly, and many people have no obvious symptoms in the early stages.
Common Early Signs and Symptoms
Frequent urination: Needing to pee more often—especially at night—happens as your kidneys try to flush out extra sugar from your blood.
Increased thirst and dry mouth: High blood sugar pulls fluid from your tissues, leaving you unusually thirsty even after drinking.
Constant fatigue: When your cells cannot properly absorb glucose for energy, you feel persistently tired and worn out.
Blurry vision: High blood sugar can cause temporary fluid swelling in the lenses of your eyes.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: Elevated blood sugar impairs circulation and your immune system's ability to heal wounds.
Tingling or numbness: Peripheral nerve damage can cause a burning or prickling sensation, or loss of feeling, in your hands and feet.
Unexplained weight changes: Your body may lose weight unexpectedly if it starts burning fat and muscle for energy, or experience weight gain linked to insulin resistance.
Frequent infections: Higher sugar levels encourage the growth of bacteria and fungi, leading to common skin, gum, or urinary tract infections.
Darkened skin patches: Velvety, dark patches around the neck, armpits, or groin (acanthosis nigricans) can be a sign of insulin resistance.
When to Get Tested
Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using simple blood tests through a healthcare provider, such as a fasting plasma glucose test or an A1C test (which measures your average blood sugar over the past two to three months).
You can learn more about diagnostic criteria and guidelines at the Cleveland Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Guide or review clinical overviews from the Mayo Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Page.

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed by a healthcare provider using specific blood tests that measure your blood sugar or average glucose levels.
Key Diagnostic Blood Tests
A1C Test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months.
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: Measures your blood sugar after you do not eat or drink anything (except water) for at least 8 hours.
Random Plasma Glucose Test: Measures your blood sugar at any time of day, regardless of when you last ate.
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): Measures your blood sugar before and 2 hours after you drink a special sugary liquid.
Confirmation and Screening
Repeat Testing: Except in cases of a random test with clear symptoms, doctors usually confirm a diabetes diagnosis by repeating one of the tests on a different day.
Who Should Get Tested: The American Diabetes Association recommends screening for all adults age 35 or older (or age 45 and older), as well as younger adults who are overweight or have additional risk factors like high blood pressure or a family history of diabetes. You can evaluate your personal risk using the ADA 60-Second Risk Test.

Type 2 diabetes treatment focuses on lowering blood sugar, managing weight, and preventing organ or heart damage. Doctors use a step-by-step approach that combines healthy habits, oral or injectable medications, and sometimes surgery.
1. Lifestyle Changes (The Foundation)
Healthy Eating: Choose non-starchy vegetables, lean proteins, and complex carbohydrates while cutting back on added sugars and refined grains.
Physical Activity: Incorporating regular moderate-to-vigorous exercise (such as brisk walking) plus muscle-strengthening sessions supports overall metabolic health.
Weight Management: Losing a modest percentage of your body weight can improve how your body uses insulin and help lower blood pressure and cholesterol.
2. Oral Medications (Pills)
If diet and exercise are not enough, doctors usually prescribe pills first. Many people take a combination of these drugs:
Metformin (Biguanide): This is almost always the first-line medication. It lowers how much glucose your liver makes and helps your cells respond better to insulin.
Sulfonylureas: Medications like glipizide and glimepiride make the pancreas release more insulin.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: These pills help your kidneys remove extra sugar through your urine, and they can also protect your heart and kidneys.
DPP-4 Inhibitors (Gliptins): These help block digestive enzymes to keep blood sugar from spiking after meals.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): Drugs like pioglitazone make muscle and fat cells more sensitive to insulin.
Meglitinides: Fast-acting pills taken around meal times to trigger a quick release of insulin.
3. Injectable Medications (Non-Insulin)
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: Injectable drugs (such as semaglutide or liraglutide) slow down digestion, help you feel full, encourage your pancreas to release insulin when needed, and often assist with weight loss.
Dual GLP-1/GIP Agonists: Newer combination injectables that provide even stronger blood sugar and weight management.
4. Insulin Therapy
If your pancreas eventually produces very little insulin, or if other medications do not keep your numbers in range, your doctor may prescribe insulin injections (long-acting, short-acting, or a mix) or an insulin pump.
5. Surgical & Procedural Options
Weight Loss (Bariatric) Surgery: Recommended for individuals with severe obesity, this surgery can dramatically improve blood sugar control and sometimes put type 2 diabetes into remission.

Common and serious side effects of Jardiance (empagliflozin) are tied to how the medication helps your kidneys remove excess sugar through urine.
Common Side Effects
Urinary tract infections (UTIs): Symptoms include burning, urgency, frequency, cloudy or bloody urine, and lower back or side pain.
Genital yeast infections: Vaginal yeast infections in women (thick white discharge, itching, burning) and fungal infections of the penis or scrotum in men (redness, itching, swelling, strong odor).
Increased urination: Needing to pee more often or in larger amounts.
Mild symptoms: Increased thirst, mild nausea, or joint pain.
Serious Side Effects
Dehydration and low blood pressure: Can cause dizziness, lightheadedness, weakness, or fainting, especially when standing up. Risk is higher if you take water pills (diuretics), are 65 or older, have kidney disease, or follow a low-salt diet.
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): A life-threatening buildup of acid and ketones in the blood—which can happen even if blood sugar is under 250 mg/dL. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach-area pain, unusual fatigue, trouble breathing, and fruity-smelling breath.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): More likely if Jardiance is taken alongside other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas. Symptoms include shakiness, fast heartbeat, confusion, sweating, and dizziness.
Serious kidney infections: Such as pyelonephritis or urosepsis.
Necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier's gangrene): A rare, severe, and life-threatening bacterial infection of the tissue under the skin in the perineal area (between the anus and genitals).
Lower limb amputations: An increased risk of toe or leg amputations has been observed, particularly in people with a history of amputation, peripheral vascular disease, or diabetic foot ulcers.
Severe allergic reactions: Including rash, hives, or swelling of the face, lips, tongue, and throat.

Current clinical guidelines (such as the American Diabetes Association) recommend SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists as co-first-line or preferred options in patients with type 2 diabetes who have or are at high risk for cardiorenal disease, rather than picking one class blindly.

GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (Mostly injectable therapies like semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide; oral semaglutide is also available):

High blood pressure (hypertension) is diagnosed when your blood pressure readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.
Blood pressure is measured with two numbers:
Systolic (top number): Measures pressure in your arteries when your heart beats.
Diastolic (bottom number): Measures pressure in your arteries when your heart rests between beats.
Blood Pressure Categories
According to guidelines from the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, blood pressure is categorized as follows:
Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 1 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 130–139 mm Hg systolic or 80–89 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 2 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 140 mm Hg or higher systolic or 90 mm Hg or higher diastolic
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic (If higher than 180/120 mm Hg with symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, or weakness, seek emergency medical care immediately by calling 911).

Treatment options for hypertension (high blood pressure) combine lifestyle changes and prescription medications to lower blood pressure and protect against heart disease, stroke, and kidney damage.
1. Lifestyle Modifications
Doctors recommend heart-healthy lifestyle changes for all people with high blood pressure, and sometimes these changes are enough to control stage 1 hypertension:
Diet: Follow the DASH Eating Plan, which focuses on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy, and low sodium (salt) intake.
Weight Management: Lose extra body weight or maintain a healthy weight to reduce the workload on your heart.
Physical Activity: Get regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming.
Habits: Quit smoking or using tobacco, and limit alcohol intake (no more than one drink per day for women and two for men).
Sleep & Stress: Aim for at least 7 hours of quality sleep per night and manage stress levels.
2. Blood Pressure Medications
When lifestyle changes do not lower blood pressure sufficiently—or if you have a high cardiovascular risk, diabetes, or kidney disease—healthcare providers prescribe one or more Types of Blood Pressure Medications:
Thiazide Diuretics: "Water pills" that help your body get rid of excess sodium and water.
ACE Inhibitors (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors): Medications like lisinopril that relax and widen blood vessels.
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): Medications like losartan that block the action of chemicals that narrow blood vessels.
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Medications like amlodipine that prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells to let vessels relax.
Other Options: Beta-blockers, alpha-blockers, or central-acting agents may be added depending on specific heart conditions or if you have Resistant Hypertension.
3. Procedural Options
Renal Denervation: A minimally invasive, FDA-approved procedure that can help lower blood pressure in patients with uncontrolled or resistant hypertension who do not respond well to medications.

Both ACE inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, ending in -pril like lisinopril) and ARBs (angiotensin II receptor blockers, ending in -sartan like losartan) are top-tier, class I first-line medications for treating high blood pressure .
Effectiveness
Blood Pressure and Heart Protection: They work equally well at lowering blood pressure and protecting the heart, kidneys, and blood vessels.
Cardiovascular Outcomes: Large-scale studies show no significant difference between ACE inhibitors and ARBs in preventing heart attacks, strokes, heart failure, or major cardiovascular events.
Side Effects & Safety Profile
Side Effect Differences: ARBs have a better tolerability profile and lower rates of side effects.
Dry Cough: ACE inhibitors block the breakdown of bradykinin, which causes a nagging dry cough in about 10% of patients. This happens much less often with ARBs (around 3%).
Angioedema: ACE inhibitors carry a higher risk of angioedema (dangerous swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat) compared to ARBs.
Other Risks: ACE inhibitors have also been linked to higher rates of acute pancreatitis and gastrointestinal bleeding in comparative data.
Shared Precautions: Both classes can raise blood potassium levels (hyperkalemia) and are strictly contraindicated during pregnancy due to risks to the fetus.
Current Guidance
Major medical guidelines (such as the ACC/AHA and ESC/ESH) list both ACE inhibitors and ARBs as equally valid first-line choices.
However, growing real-world evidence and clinical preference lean toward starting with an ARB first to avoid side effects like the dry cough or angioedema.
If you are already taking an ACE inhibitor and tolerating it well, doctors generally do not need to switch you.

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over years, and many people have no symptoms in the early stages. When early signs do appear, they are often subtle and can be easy to dismiss.
Common Early Signs and Symptoms
Frequent urination (polyuria): You visit the bathroom more often than usual, especially at night, as your kidneys try to flush out extra glucose from your blood.
Excessive thirst (polydipsia): Because you lose more fluid through frequent urination, you feel constantly thirsty.
Persistent fatigue: Your cells cannot properly absorb glucose to use for fuel, leaving you feeling tired and worn out even after resting.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar can cause temporary fluid shifts and swelling in the lenses of your eyes.
Slow-healing sores or cuts: Elevated blood sugar impairs circulation and weakens your immune response, making minor injuries take much longer to heal.
Tingling or numbness: Mild nerve irritation or damage (peripheral neuropathy) can cause a pins-and-needles sensation, tingling, or numbness in your hands or feet.
Unexplained weight changes: Your body may burn fat and muscle for energy instead of glucose, leading to unexpected weight loss, or you might experience insulin-related weight gain (especially around the abdomen).
Frequent infections: Bacteria and fungi thrive on extra sugar, leading to recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs), yeast infections, or skin issues.
Darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin can form in body folds like the neck, armpits, or groin as a sign of heavy insulin resistance.
How to Get Checked
Because type 2 diabetes is so quiet early on, routine screening is important if you are over 45 or have risk factors like a family history, high blood pressure, or a sedentary lifestyle.
A doctor can diagnose it using simple blood tests through the Cleveland Clinic Health Guide or your primary care provider:
Fasting plasma glucose test (126 mg/dL or higher)
A1C test measuring average blood sugar over 2 to 3 months (6.5% or higher)
Random plasma glucose test (200 mg/dL or higher)

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure your blood glucose or average blood sugar levels over time.
Diagnostic Criteria
According to guidelines from the American Diabetes Association, type 2 diabetes is diagnosed if you meet any of the following thresholds:
Hemoglobin A1C Test: 6.5% or higher (measures average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months).
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher (taken after fasting with no caloric intake for at least 8 hours).
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher (measured 2 hours after drinking a 75-gram glucose solution).
Random Plasma Glucose Test: 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher in someone who is having classic symptoms of high blood sugar (such as frequent urination, extreme thirst, or unexplained weight loss).
Confirmation Testing
Repeat Testing: If you do not have classic, severe symptoms of high blood sugar, doctors usually require a second abnormal test result (either repeating the same test or using a different test) to confirm the diagnosis.
Prediabetes Range: If your numbers fall between normal and diabetic levels, you may be diagnosed with prediabetes (A1C of 5.7%–6.4%, fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dL, or 2-hour OGTT of 140–199 mg/dL).

Treatment for type 2 diabetes focuses on keeping blood sugar levels in a healthy range, protecting organs, and managing related health conditions like high blood pressure or high cholesterol.
1. Lifestyle Changes
Healthy Eating: Focus on lean proteins, non-starchy vegetables, complex carbohydrates, and good fats while limiting excess sugars and refined starches.
Physical Activity: Aim for regular movement, such as 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise per week, plus muscle-strengthening workouts.
Weight Management: Losing even 5% to 10% of your body weight can significantly improve how your body handles insulin and regulates blood sugar.
2. Oral Medications
If lifestyle changes are not enough to reach target glucose levels, healthcare providers typically prescribe pills taken by mouth. The American Diabetes Association provides detailed guides on these medications: American Diabetes Association +2
Metformin: Most often the first medicine prescribed; it lowers glucose production in the liver and helps the body use insulin better.
Sulfonylureas: Examples include glipizide and glimepiride; they stimulate the pancreas to make more insulin.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): Examples include pioglitazone (Actos); they help insulin work better in fat and muscle tissue.
DPP-4 Inhibitors (Gliptins): They block an enzyme to help enhance the body's natural blood-sugar-lowering hormones.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: They help the kidneys remove excess glucose from the body through urine.

GLP-1 Receptor Agonists & Dual GLP-1/GIP Agonists: These are injectable medications that boost insulin secretion during meals, slow digestion, promote fullness, and can support weight loss and heart health.

If the body stops producing enough natural insulin over time, or if other medications are not enough, doctors may prescribe insulin therapy via injections or an insulin pump. Options include long-acting (basal) and short-acting (mealtime) insulins.

Blood Glucose Tracking: Using a home blood glucose meter or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) helps track how food, activity, and medicine affect your body.
Weight Loss (Bariatric) Surgery: For individuals with severe obesity and difficult-to-manage type 2 diabetes, metabolic or weight-loss surgery can be a very effective option to improve or even remit the condition.

Choosing between an SGLT2 inhibitor and a GLP-1 receptor agonist as a first-line or early-line therapy for type 2 diabetes depends on a patient's specific health profile, primary risk factors, and treatment goals, according to guidelines from the American Diabetes Association .
Core Comparison at a Glance
When to Choose SGLT2 Inhibitors First
Heart Failure: If the patient has heart failure (especially with reduced ejection fraction), SGLT2 inhibitors are strongly preferred due to proven reductions in heart failure hospitalizations.
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): If the patient has established CKD (down to low eGFR thresholds), SGLT2 inhibitors provide the strongest evidence for slowing kidney function decline.
Preference for Pills: Patients who prefer taking an oral daily pill over self-injecting a medication.
When to Choose GLP-1 Receptor Agonists First
Higher A1c or Weight-Loss Goals: GLP-1s provide more potent blood sugar (A1c) lowering and significantly greater weight loss compared to SGLT2 inhibitors.
Stroke Prevention & High ASCVD Risk: If the primary vascular threat is atherosclerotic disease or a high risk of stroke, GLP-1s show an advantage.
Convenience of Dosing: Many modern GLP-1s are taken just once a week via sub-cutaneous pen injection.
Can You Use Both?
Yes. Guidelines and clinical evidence show that combining an SGLT2 inhibitor and a GLP-1 receptor agonist offers complementary, additive benefits for heart, kidney, and metabolic control if a single agent is insufficient (though insurance coverage and cost can be a barrier).

High blood pressure (hypertension) is usually a "silent killer" because it rarely causes any noticeable warning signs. Most people can live with high blood pressure for years without feeling anything unusual.
When Symptoms Do Appear
Symptoms usually only show up if your blood pressure spikes to dangerously high levels (a hypertensive crisis, typically 180/120 mm Hg or higher).
Signs of a severe spike or hypertensive emergency can include:
Severe headaches or pressure in the head
Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Chest pain or tightness
Blurty vision or other vision changes
Dizziness, confusion, or fatigue
Nosebleeds or blood spots in the eyes
Numbness or weakness
How to Know Your Numbers
Because you cannot rely on how you feel, regular checks are essential. You can learn more about blood pressure ranges through the American Heart Association or read the detailed overview on Mayo Clinic.
Normal: Less than 120/80 mm Hg
Elevated: 120–129 / less than 80 mm Hg
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130–139 / 80–89 mm Hg
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140/90 mm Hg or higher
Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180/120 mm Hg (Seek emergency medical help immediately if paired with symptoms like chest pain or shortness of breath)

High blood pressure (hypertension) is officially diagnosed when your readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.
Blood pressure is measured with two numbers:
Systolic (top number): The pressure in your arteries when your heart beats.
Diastolic (bottom number): The pressure in your arteries when your heart rests between beats.
Blood Pressure Categories
The American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention break down blood pressure into these ranges:
Elevated: Not yet high blood pressure, but a sign that you are at risk of developing it.
Stage 1 Hypertension: Doctors usually recommend lifestyle changes and may consider medication depending on your heart disease or stroke risk.
Stage 2 Hypertension: Typically requires a combination of medication and lifestyle adjustments.
Hypertensive Crisis (Above 180/120): Wait 5 minutes and test again. If it is still this high and you have symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, or vision changes, call 911 immediately.

Treating high blood pressure (hypertension) usually involves a mix of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, if needed, prescription medications. The standard treatment goal for most adults is a blood pressure reading of less than 130/80 mm Hg.
1. Lifestyle Modifications
Doctors recommend lifestyle changes for everyone with high blood pressure. These changes can lower your numbers or reduce the amount of medication you need:
Eat a heart-healthy diet: Follow the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet, which focuses on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fats.
Reduce sodium (salt): Aim to lower your daily salt intake (ideally under 1,500 to 2,000 mg per day).
Exercise regularly: Get at least 30 minutes of aerobic activity (such as brisk walking) most days of the week.
Manage your weight: Losing extra body weight takes stress off your heart and blood vessels.
Limit alcohol and avoid smoking: Cut back on alcohol and quit smoking or using tobacco products, which narrow blood vessels.
Get quality sleep: Aim for 7 or more hours of sleep per night to help manage stress hormones.
2. Medication Options
When lifestyle changes alone do not lower blood pressure enough—or if you have stage 2 hypertension or higher health risks—your doctor may prescribe one or more medications.
The four main classes of first-line blood pressure medications include:
ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril, ramipril): Keep blood vessels from narrowing.
ARBs / Angiotensin II receptor blockers (e.g., losartan, valsartan): Relax and widen blood vessels by blocking specific chemical signals.
Calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells, allowing vessels to relax.
Thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide): Help your body get rid of excess water and sodium (salt) through urine.
Other or second-line medications (such as beta-blockers, alpha-blockers, or central-acting agents like clonidine) may be added depending on your age, race, or other conditions like heart disease, kidney disease, or diabetes. Over 50% of people with hypertension need a combination of two or more drugs to reach their target.

Both ACE inhibitors and ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) are recognized as equally effective first-line therapy options for lowering blood pressure in essential hypertension.
Core Similarities
Blood Pressure Efficacy: Both classes lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure with comparable effectiveness.
Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS) Inhibition: Both target the same pathway to promote vasodilation and reduce cardiac workload.
Guideline Standing: Major medical guidelines (such as the ACC/AHA and ESC/ESH) list both as top-tier, class I first-line choices.
Key Differences
Side Effects:
Preference Shift: Recent real-world comparative studies and clinical reviews increasingly favor starting with an ARB over an ACE inhibitor due to the superior safety and adherence profile.
Mechanism: ACE inhibitors stop the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, whereas ARBs block angiotensin II from binding to its cellular receptors.

Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) occurs when the tiny arteries in your lungs thicken and narrow, forcing the right side of your heart to work much harder to pump blood.
Early Signs and Symptoms
In the early stages, PAH often causes no symptoms at all. When symptoms do start, they are usually mild and easy to confuse with other heart or lung conditions like asthma or COPD:
Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially during exercise or everyday tasks like climbing stairs or walking to the store
Fatigue and general weakness
Lightheadedness or dizziness, particularly with exertion
Advanced Symptoms
As the right side of the heart becomes strained or begins to fail, more noticeable and serious symptoms develop:
Chest pressure or pain
Swelling (edema) in the ankles, legs, feet, or abdomen (due to fluid retention)
Fainting or syncopy (passing out during physical activity)
Heart palpitations or a racing, pounding heartbeat
Bluish lips or skin (cyanosis) from low oxygen levels
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or hoarseness in rare, advanced cases
Because these warning signs develop slowly and overlap with other conditions, getting an accurate diagnosis requires specialized testing such as an echocardiogram or right heart catheterization through the American Lung Association.

Opsumit (macitentan) can cause several common and serious side effects. It is prescribed to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).
Common Side Effects
Headache (reported in about 14% of patients)
Nasopharyngitis or common cold / stuffy nose (up to 20%)
Bronchitis or upper respiratory tract infections (11% to 15%)
Anemia (low red blood cell count, around 13%)
Urinary tract infection (UTI)
Influenza-like symptoms
Serious Side Effects & Warnings
Serious Birth Defects / Embryo-Fetal Toxicity: Opsumit can cause severe harm or death to an unborn fetus. Women who can become pregnant must have a negative pregnancy test before starting treatment and use reliable, dual contraception during therapy and for one month after stopping.
Liver Damage / Hepatotoxicity: Opsumit can affect liver function. Doctors check liver enzymes before starting treatment. Seek immediate medical care for signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe upper right stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting.
Fluid Retention and Swelling: Peripheral edema (swelling of the hands, legs, or feet) or fluid buildup can occur, usually during the first few weeks of treatment.
Decreased Red Blood Cells (Anemia): Significant drops in hemoglobin can happen early in treatment and may occasionally require a blood transfusion.
Decreased Sperm Count: Opsumit may reduce sperm counts and impact male fertility.

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over several years, and many people experience very mild or no early symptoms.
Early Warning Signs
Frequent urination: Needing to go to the bathroom more often, especially at night, as your kidneys try to flush out excess sugar.
Increased thirst: Feeling unusually thirsty or dry-mouthed because fluid loss from frequent urination leaves you dehydrated.
Persistent fatigue: Feeling overly tired or weak because your body's cells cannot properly use glucose for energy.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar causing fluid to shift and swell the lenses of your eyes.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: Poor circulation and a weakened immune response slowing down your body's ability to repair skin damage.
Tingling or numbness: Early nerve irritation or damage (neuropathy) causing pins and needles or loss of feeling in the hands or feet.
Unexplained weight loss: Losing weight without trying as your body burns muscle and fat for fuel.
Darkened skin patches: Velvety, dark patches of skin (acanthosis nigricans) in body folds like the neck, armpits, or groin, which can signal insulin resistance.
Frequent infections: Recurring urinary tract infections, yeast infections, or skin sores.
How It Is Diagnosed
Because early signs can be subtle or easy to miss, doctors confirm type 2 diabetes using simple blood tests through the Cleveland Clinic or your primary care provider:
A1C test: Measures your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months (6.5% or higher indicates diabetes).
Fasting plasma glucose test: Checks your blood sugar after an 8-hour fast (126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes).
Random plasma glucose test: Checks your blood sugar at any time of day (200 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes).

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests evaluated by a healthcare provider. In the absence of clear symptoms, an abnormal test result is typically repeated on a second day to confirm the diagnosis.
Diagnostic Criteria
Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed when any of the following thresholds are met, according to guidelines from the American Diabetes Association:
Hemoglobin A1C Test (HbA1c): 6.5% or higher (measures average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months).
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher (after fasting for at least 8 hours).
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher (measured 2 hours after drinking a 75-gram glucose solution).
Random Plasma Glucose Test: 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher (tested anytime in someone who is experiencing classic symptoms of high blood sugar like frequent urination, extreme thirst, or unexplained weight loss).
Prediabetes Range
Before type 2 diabetes develops, blood sugar levels are often elevated but not high enough to meet the diabetes threshold:
A1C: 5.7% to 6.4%
Fasting Blood Glucose: 100 to 125 mg/dL (5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L)
2-Hour OGTT: 140 to 199 mg/dL (7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L)

Treatment for type 2 diabetes focuses on keeping blood sugar levels in a healthy range, protecting organs, and managing related health conditions like high blood pressure or high cholesterol.
1. Lifestyle Changes
Healthy Eating: Focus on lean proteins, non-starchy vegetables, complex carbohydrates, and good fats while limiting excess sugars and refined starches.
Physical Activity: Aim for regular movement, such as 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise per week, plus muscle-strengthening workouts.
Weight Management: Losing even 5% to 10% of your body weight can significantly improve how your body handles insulin and regulates blood sugar.
2. Oral Medications
If lifestyle changes are not enough to reach target glucose levels, healthcare providers typically prescribe pills taken by mouth. The American Diabetes Association provides detailed guides on these medications: American Diabetes Association +2
Metformin: Most often the first medicine prescribed; it lowers glucose production in the liver and helps the body use insulin better.
Sulfonylureas: Examples include glipizide and glimepiride; they stimulate the pancreas to make more insulin.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): Examples include pioglitazone (Actos); they help insulin work better in fat and muscle tissue.
DPP-4 Inhibitors (Gliptins): They block an enzyme to help enhance the body's natural blood-sugar-lowering hormones.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: They help the kidneys remove excess glucose from the body through urine.
3. Injectable Non-Insulin Medications
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists & Dual GLP-1/GIP Agonists: These are injectable medications that boost insulin secretion during meals, slow digestion, promote fullness, and can support weight loss and heart health.
4. Insulin Therapy
If the body stops producing enough natural insulin over time, or if other medications are not enough, doctors may prescribe insulin therapy via injections or an insulin pump. Options include long-acting (basal) and short-acting (mealtime) insulins.
5. Blood Sugar Monitoring and Surgery
Blood Glucose Tracking: Using a home blood glucose meter or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) helps track how food, activity, and medicine affect your body.
Weight Loss (Bariatric) Surgery: For individuals with severe obesity and difficult-to-manage type 2 diabetes, metabolic or weight-loss surgery can be a very effective option to improve or even remit the condition.

Jardiance (empagliflozin) is a medication that helps your kidneys remove excess sugar through your urine. Because of how it works, it can cause several common and serious side effects.
Common Side Effects
Increased urination: You will likely need to pee more often. Taking your dose in the morning can help prevent getting up during the night.
Urinary tract infections (UTIs): Symptoms include a burning sensation when you pee, an urgent or frequent need to go, cloudy or bloody urine, or lower back/side pain.
Genital yeast infections: These happen in both women (vaginal itching, burning, thick white discharge) and men (redness, irritation, or rash around the penis or scrotum).
Increased thirst and mild dehydration: Extra fluid loss can leave you feeling unusually thirsty.
Serious Side Effects (Seek Medical Attention)
Dehydration and low blood pressure: Can cause dizziness, lightheadedness, weakness, or fainting, especially when standing up. Risk is higher if you take water pills (diuretics), are over 65, or have kidney issues.
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): A dangerous buildup of acid in the blood—which can happen even if your blood sugar is not very high. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, unusual tiredness, trouble breathing, or a fruity odor on your breath.
Low blood sugar (Hypoglycemia): More likely if you take Jardiance along with other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas. Symptoms include shaking, sweating, fast heartbeat, confusion, and headache.
Severe urinary tract or kidney infections: Infections that spread to the kidneys or blood (pyelonephritis, urosepsis).
Necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier’s gangrene): A rare, life-threatening bacterial infection of the tissue under the skin in the perineum (area between the genitals and anus) causing severe pain, redness, swelling, and fever.
Lower limb amputations: An increased risk has been observed with SGLT2 inhibitors, particularly for people with a history of prior amputations, peripheral vascular disease, or diabetic foot ulcers.
Serious allergic reactions: Hives, or swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat causing trouble swallowing or breathing.

Neither SGLT2 inhibitors nor GLP-1 receptor agonists are traditionally recommended as first-line monotherapy for type 2 diabetes; metformin remains the universal first-line pharmacological treatment alongside lifestyle changes .
However, both classes are frequently prioritized as second-line agents—or even initiated alongside metformin—based on specific patient comorbidities, cardiovascular risk, and organ protection needs.
Core Differences in Selection
Instead of choosing one universally, medical guidelines (such as the American Diabetes Association) guide selection based on what dominant health condition the patient has:
Choose an SGLT2 Inhibitor (e.g., empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin) if the patient has heart failure (especially with reduced ejection fraction) or chronic kidney disease (CKD). SGLT2i provide superior reductions in heart failure hospitalizations and slow the progression of kidney disease.
Choose a GLP-1 Receptor Agonist (e.g., semaglutide, liraglutide) if the patient has predominant atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), high risk of stroke/MACE (major adverse cardiovascular events), or needs more potent HbA1c lowering and weight loss. GLP-1s are generally more powerful for blood sugar reduction and substantial weight reduction.
Comparison at a Glance
Combination Therapy
In many patients with established cardiorenal disease or inadequate glycemic control, clinical guidelines increasingly support combining both an SGLT2 inhibitor and a GLP-1 receptor agonist, as their mechanisms of action and protective benefits are additive rather than overlapping.
For detailed guidance tailored to specific health profiles, you can review the American Diabetes Association Standards of Care.

High blood pressure (hypertension) is often called the "silent killer" because it typically has no signs or symptoms. Most people with high blood pressure feel completely fine and can live with it for years without knowing.
When Symptoms Do Appear (Dangerously High Blood Pressure / Hypertensive Crisis)
Symptoms generally do not show up until blood pressure reaches dangerously high levels—typically a reading of 180/120 mm Hg or higher.
If your blood pressure is extremely high, you may experience:
Severe headaches
Blurry vision or other sudden changes in eyesight
Shortness of breath
Chest pain
Dizziness or lightheadedness
Fatigue or confusion
Nosebleeds
What to Do in a Hypertensive Emergency
According to the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention:
Wait at least 1 minute and take your blood pressure again if your reading is above 180/120 mm Hg.
If the second reading is just as high and you have any warning signs—such as chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, change in vision, or difficulty speaking—call 911 immediately.
If your reading is above 180/120 mm Hg but you do not have any of these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider right away for guidance.
How to Know Your Numbers
Because you cannot rely on how you feel, regular screening is essential. Adults should have their blood pressure checked at least once a year during regular medical visits, or more frequently if recommended by a doctor. According to guidelines from the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, high blood pressure (hypertension) starts when your readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.
Blood pressure is measured using two numbers: systolic (the top number, measuring pressure when the heart beats) and diastolic (the bottom number, measuring pressure when the heart rests between beats).
Blood Pressure Categories
Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130–139 mm Hg systolic or 80–89 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140 mm Hg or higher systolic or 90 mm Hg or higher diastolic
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic
What the Stages Mean
Elevated: Not yet high blood pressure, but a warning sign to adopt heart-healthy habits to prevent hypertension.
Stage 1: Doctors typically recommend lifestyle changes and may consider medication based on your overall heart disease or stroke risk.
Stage 2: Usually treated with a combination of lifestyle changes and blood pressure medication.
Severe / Crisis: If readings exceed 180/120 mm Hg, rest for five minutes and retest. If it remains that high and you have symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, or vision changes, call 911 immediately (hypertensive emergency). If you have no symptoms, contact your healthcare provider right away.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is typically managed through a combination of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications.
Lifestyle Modifications
Adopting healthy habits is the first step in lowering blood pressure and can sometimes reduce the need for or amount of medication:
Dietary Approaches (DASH): Follow the DASH Eating Plan, which emphasizes vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on sodium (salt).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling.
Weight Management: Lose excess weight if you are overweight or obese to reduce strain on your heart and blood vessels.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce alcohol consumption and stop smoking or using tobacco, which immediately constricts blood vessels and raises heart rate.
Stress and Sleep: Practice stress-reduction techniques and aim for at least 7 hours of quality sleep per night.
First-Line Medications
When lifestyle modifications alone do not lower blood pressure sufficiently—or if you have a high 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease—doctors typically prescribe one or more classes of blood pressure drugs:
Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors: Relax blood vessels to keep them from narrowing (e.g., lisinopril, benazepril).
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Block the action of chemicals that tighten blood vessels (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells, allowing vessels to relax (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help your body get rid of excess sodium and water, reducing fluid volume in the blood; thiazide diuretics are most common (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide).
Treatment Approaches
Single vs. Multi-Drug Therapy: Stage 1 hypertension is often managed with a single medication, while Stage 2 hypertension or higher risk profiles frequently require two or more medications combined—sometimes in a single pill for convenience.
Target Goals: For most adults, the general treatment goal is a blood pressure reading of less than 130/80 mm Hg.
Resistant Hypertension: If blood pressure remains high despite taking three or more medications (including a diuretic), a healthcare provider will investigate underlying causes and adjust the regimen or consider specialized interventions.

Losartan is a prescription medication in the angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) class used to treat high blood pressure, protect the kidneys in type 2 diabetes, and lower the risk of stroke.
Common and Mild Side Effects
These effects are usually mild and often improve as your body adjusts to the medication:
Dizziness or lightheadedness (especially when standing up quickly from a sitting or lying position)
Fatigue or tiredness
Headache
Upper respiratory tract infections (such as a stuffy or runny nose, or sore throat)
Digestive issues (nausea, diarrhea, or mild stomach upset)
Back or joint pain and muscle cramps
Serious Side Effects (Seek Medical Attention)
Contact your doctor or seek emergency care right away if you experience:
Allergic reactions / Angioedema: Sudden swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat, eyes, hands, or feet, or difficulty breathing or swallowing (a medical emergency).
High potassium levels (hyperkalemia): Muscle weakness, confusion, numbness or tingling, or a fast or irregular heartbeat.
Low blood pressure (hypotension): Severe dizziness, fainting, or blurry vision.
Kidney problems: A major decrease in the amount of urine, blood in the urine, or unexplained swelling in the legs, ankles, or hands.
Liver issues: Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice) or severe upper stomach pain.
Important Safety Tips
Stand up slowly: To prevent dizziness or fainting spells when getting out of bed or a chair, transition slowly.
Avoid potassium supplements: Do not use potassium-containing salt substitutes or supplements unless directed by your healthcare provider, as losartan can raise potassium levels.
Pregnancy warning: Losartan should not be taken during pregnancy, as it can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby.

Both ACE inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors) and ARBs (angiotensin II receptor blockers) are recognized as major first-line drug classes for managing high blood pressure (hypertension), alongside calcium channel blockers and thiazide diuretics .
Key Similarities
Blood Pressure Efficacy: Both classes lower blood pressure and reduce systemic vascular resistance to a similar extent by targeting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).
Cardiovascular & Renal Protection: Both offer significant benefits in protecting the heart and kidneys, especially in patients with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or heart failure.
Combinations: They must never be taken together in combination due to a higher risk of hyperkalemia and kidney injury.
Key Differences & Why ARBs Are Often Preferred First-Line
Mechanism of Action:
Side Effect Profile:
Guideline & Clinical Shift: While traditional guidelines (such as ACC/AHA and ESC/ESH) historically placed ACE inhibitors and ARBs on equal footing, large comparative studies (published via JAMA Network and Annals of Internal Medicine ) show identical cardiovascular efficacy with a much more favorable side effect and adherence profile for ARBs. As a result, many clinicians now preferentially start with an ARB.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which strains the right side of the heart.
Early and Common Symptoms
In the early stages, PAH may cause no noticeable symptoms. As it progresses, symptoms often mimic other heart or lung conditions (such as asthma or deconditioning), including:
Shortness of breath (dyspnea), initially during exercise or physical exertion and eventually while at rest
Fatigue and weakness or a feeling of heavy limbs
Chest pain, pressure, or tightness caused by an overworked, strained heart
Dizziness or lightheadedness, particularly during physical activity
Heart palpitations or a fast, pounding pulse
Progressive and Later-Stage Symptoms
As pressure builds and the right side of the heart faces increasing difficulty pumping blood, more severe signs can develop:
Swelling (edema) in the ankles, feet, legs, or abdomen due to fluid retention
Fainting spells (syncope) with exertion
Bluish or gray lips and skin (cyanosis) from low oxygen levels in the blood
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or hoarseness (from an enlarged pulmonary artery pressing on chest nerves) in advanced cases
You can learn more about how specialists evaluate these signs through the American Lung Association PAH Guide or review broad clinical overviews via the Mayo Clinic Pulmonary Hypertension Overview.

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over months or years, and many people have no obvious symptoms in the early stages. When early warning signs do appear, they are often subtle and easy to attribute to stress, aging, or a busy lifestyle.
Common Early Signs and Symptoms
Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar builds up in the blood, forcing the kidneys to work overtime to filter and absorb the excess glucose, which draws fluid from your tissues and leads to frequent bathroom trips and dehydration.
Persistent fatigue and weakness: When cells cannot effectively absorb and use glucose for energy, you may feel unusually tired or worn out even after resting.
Increased hunger: Without enough glucose entering your cells, your body may constantly signal that it needs fuel, leading to sudden or heightened hunger.
Blurred vision: Fluctuating or high blood sugar can cause temporary swelling in the lenses of the eyes.
Slow-healing cuts, sores, or bruises: Impaired circulation and minor nerve damage reduce the body's natural ability to repair skin and fight off minor injuries.
Tingling or numbness: Early peripheral nerve damage (neuropathy) can cause a pins-and-needles sensation, pain, or numbness in the hands or feet.
Recurrent infections: High sugar levels create an environment where bacteria and fungi thrive, leading to frequent urinary tract infections (UTIs), yeast infections, or skin issues.
Darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin appearing in body folds—most commonly around the neck, armpits, or groin—can be an outward sign of insulin resistance.
Unexplained weight changes: While weight gain (especially around the abdomen) is closely linked to insulin resistance, some individuals experience unexpected weight loss when the body begins burning muscle and fat for energy instead.
How It Is Diagnosed
Because symptoms can be silent, healthcare providers rely on simple blood tests to confirm whether you have prediabetes or type 2 diabetes:
Fasting plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar after an 8-hour fast; a result of 126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.
A1C test: Measures average blood sugar levels over the past 2 to 3 months; a result of 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes.
Random plasma glucose test: Checked at any time of day; a result of 200 mg/dL or higher (alongside symptoms) points to diabetes.

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests administered in a medical setting.
Main Diagnostic Blood Tests
A1C Test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months. A result of 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes.
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: Measures your blood sugar after fasting (not eating or drinking anything except water) for at least 8 hours. A result of 126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): Measures your blood sugar before and 2 hours after you drink a special sugary liquid. A 2-hour blood sugar level of 200 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.

Treatment for type 2 diabetes focuses on lowering and stabilizing blood sugar levels through a combination of lifestyle changes, medications, and regular monitoring.
1. Lifestyle Changes
Healthy Eating: Focus on non-starchy vegetables, lean proteins, complex carbohydrates, and heart-healthy fats (such as the Mediterranean or DASH diets).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular exercise to improve insulin sensitivity and lower blood glucose.
Weight Management: Losing even 5% of body weight can significantly improve how the body regulates blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol. Weight loss surgery (bariatric surgery) is also an option for individuals with obesity.
Blood Sugar Monitoring: Track glucose levels at home using a standard blood glucose meter or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM).
2. Medications
When diet and exercise are not enough, healthcare providers prescribe oral or injectable medications. Detailed guides and medication classes can be reviewed via the American Diabetes Association:
Metformin (Biguanides): The standard first-line oral medication. It decreases glucose production in the liver and makes muscle and fat cells more sensitive to insulin.
Sulfonylureas: (e.g., glipizide, glimepiride, glyburide) Stimulate the pancreas to produce more insulin.
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists & GLP-1/GIP Agonists: Injectable medications that boost insulin release, slow digestion, suppress glucagon, and often support weight loss and heart/kidney health.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: Oral medications that help the kidneys remove excess glucose through urine while offering heart and kidney benefits.
DPP-4 Inhibitors (Gliptins): Oral medications that enhance incretin hormones to help lower post-meal blood sugar without causing weight gain.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): (e.g., pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) Improve insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat tissue.
Insulin Therapy: Long-acting, short-acting, or rapid-acting insulin injections or pumps may be introduced if oral and injectable medications no longer control blood sugar adequately.

Jardiance (empagliflozin) can cause common mild side effects as well as rare, serious complications.
Common Side Effects
Urinary tract infections (UTIs): Symptoms include burning, urgency, or frequent urination.
Genital yeast infections: Vaginal yeast infections in women (itching, burning, thick white discharge) and fungal infections around the penis in men.
Increased urination: Going to the bathroom more frequently because the medication flushes out extra sugar through your urine.

Seek emergency medical attention or contact your healthcare provider right away if you experience:

Kidney problems: Sudden worsening of kidney function or severe kidney infections (pyelonephritis).
Lower limb amputations: Increased risk reported in people with peripheral vascular disease or previous foot ulcers.
Serious allergic reactions: Hives, or swelling of the face, lips, tongue, and throat.

Choose SGLT2 inhibitors if: You have a history of heart failure, chronic kidney disease, or need an oral pill with lower gastrointestinal side effects .
Choose GLP-1 receptor agonists if: You need substantial weight management, have high atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk, or require strong post-meal blood sugar control.

Blood pressure is considered high (hypertension) when it is consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg, according to guidelines from the American Heart Association and the CDC.
Blood Pressure Categories
Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 1 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 130–139 mm Hg systolic or 80–89 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 2 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 140 mm Hg or higher systolic or 90 mm Hg or higher diastolic
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic (Seek emergency care if accompanied by symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, or numbness)
Understanding the Numbers
Systolic (Top number): Measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart beats.
Diastolic (Bottom number): Measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart rests between beats.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is typically managed through a combination of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications.
Lifestyle Modifications
Adopting healthy habits is the first step in lowering blood pressure and can sometimes reduce the need for or amount of medication:
Dietary Approaches (DASH): Follow the DASH Eating Plan, which emphasizes vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on sodium (salt).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling.
Weight Management: Lose excess weight if you are overweight or obese to reduce strain on your heart and blood vessels.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce alcohol consumption and stop smoking or using tobacco, which immediately constricts blood vessels and raises heart rate.
Stress and Sleep: Practice stress-reduction techniques and aim for at least 7 hours of quality sleep per night.
First-Line Medications
When lifestyle modifications alone do not lower blood pressure sufficiently—or if you have a high 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease—doctors typically prescribe one or more classes of blood pressure drugs:
Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors: Relax blood vessels to keep them from narrowing (e.g., lisinopril, benazepril).
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Block the action of chemicals that tighten blood vessels (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells, allowing vessels to relax (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help your body get rid of excess sodium and water, reducing fluid volume in the blood; thiazide diuretics are most common (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide).
Treatment Approaches
Single vs. Multi-Drug Therapy: Stage 1 hypertension is often managed with a single medication, while Stage 2 hypertension or higher risk profiles frequently require two or more medications combined—sometimes in a single pill for convenience.
Target Goals: For most adults, the general treatment goal is a blood pressure reading of less than 130/80 mm Hg.
Resistant Hypertension: If blood pressure remains high despite taking three or more medications (including a diuretic), a healthcare provider will investigate underlying causes and adjust the regimen or consider specialized interventions.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, making the right side of the heart work too hard.
In the early stages, PAH often causes no symptoms at all. As the condition progresses, signs and symptoms appear—frequently mimicking other heart or lung diseases.
Common Symptoms
Shortness of breath (dyspnea): Usually starts during exercise or routine tasks (like walking or climbing stairs) and can eventually occur at rest.
Fatigue and weakness: A deep lack of energy or heavy feeling in the body.
Chest pain or pressure: Caused by an overworked and strained right heart muscle.
Dizziness or lightheadedness: Often triggered by exertion or changes in position.
Fainting spells (syncope): Occurs when the brain temporarily receives less oxygen.
Heart palpitations: A fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat.
Advanced or Progressive Symptoms
As fluid builds up or the heart's right side begins to fail, later-stage signs may develop:
Swelling (edema): Fluid retention in the feet, ankles, legs, or abdomen (ascites).
Cyanosis: A bluish tint to the lips, fingers, or skin due to low blood oxygen levels.
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis): Rare, but can happen as pressure in the lung vessels increases.
Hoarseness: Can occur if an enlarged pulmonary artery presses on nearby chest nerves.

Opsumit (macitentan) can cause several common and serious side effects. It is prescribed to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).
Common Side Effects
Headache (reported in about 14% of patients)
Nasopharyngitis or common cold / stuffy nose (up to 20%)
Bronchitis or upper respiratory tract infections (11% to 15%)
Anemia (low red blood cell count, around 13%)
Urinary tract infection (UTI)
Influenza-like symptoms
Serious Side Effects & Warnings
Serious Birth Defects / Embryo-Fetal Toxicity: Opsumit can cause severe harm or death to an unborn fetus. Women who can become pregnant must have a negative pregnancy test before starting treatment and use reliable, dual contraception during therapy and for one month after stopping.
Liver Damage / Hepatotoxicity: Opsumit can affect liver function. Doctors check liver enzymes before starting treatment. Seek immediate medical care for signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe upper right stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting.
Fluid Retention and Swelling: Peripheral edema (swelling of the hands, legs, or feet) or fluid buildup can occur, usually during the first few weeks of treatment.
Decreased Red Blood Cells (Anemia): Significant drops in hemoglobin can happen early in treatment and may occasionally require a blood transfusion.
Decreased Sperm Count: Opsumit may reduce sperm counts and impact male fertility.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is typically managed through a combination of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications.
Lifestyle Modifications
Adopting healthy habits is the first step in lowering blood pressure and can sometimes reduce the need for or amount of medication:
Dietary Approaches (DASH): Follow the DASH Eating Plan, which emphasizes vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on sodium (salt).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling.
Weight Management: Lose excess weight if you are overweight or obese to reduce strain on your heart and blood vessels.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce alcohol consumption and stop smoking or using tobacco, which immediately constricts blood vessels and raises heart rate.
Stress and Sleep: Practice stress-reduction techniques and aim for at least 7 hours of quality sleep per night.
First-Line Medications
When lifestyle modifications alone do not lower blood pressure sufficiently—or if you have a high 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease—doctors typically prescribe one or more classes of blood pressure drugs:
Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors: Relax blood vessels to keep them from narrowing (e.g., lisinopril, benazepril).
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Block the action of chemicals that tighten blood vessels (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells, allowing vessels to relax (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help your body get rid of excess sodium and water, reducing fluid volume in the blood; thiazide diuretics are most common (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide).
Treatment Approaches
Single vs. Multi-Drug Therapy: Stage 1 hypertension is often managed with a single medication, while Stage 2 hypertension or higher risk profiles frequently require two or more medications combined—sometimes in a single pill for convenience.
Target Goals: For most adults, the general treatment goal is a blood pressure reading of less than 130/80 mm Hg.
Resistant Hypertension: If blood pressure remains high despite taking three or more medications (including a diuretic), a healthcare provider will investigate underlying causes and adjust the regimen or consider specialized interventions.

Both ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors and ARBs (angiotensin II receptor blockers) are equally recommended as class I first-line therapies for managing essential hypertension.
Efficacy
Blood Pressure Lowering: Both drug classes lower blood pressure effectively by blocking the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), with no significant difference in long-term cardiovascular event prevention or overall efficacy.
Guideline Standing: Major guidelines (such as the ACC/AHA and ESC/ESH) list ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers (CCBs), and thiazide diuretics as equal first-line options.
Key Differences & Safety Profiles
Side Effects (Cough): ACE inhibitors frequently cause a dry, persistent cough due to a buildup of bradykinin. ARBs do not block bradykinin breakdown and rarely cause this cough.
Angioedema: Both can rarely cause angioedema (tissue swelling), though the risk is higher with ACE inhibitors.
Tolerability: Real-world studies and clinical data show that ARBs generally have a better safety profile and lower discontinuation rates than ACE inhibitors, leading some clinicians to preferentially prescribe ARBs.
Combination Warning: Never combine an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together, as dual blockade increases the risk of side effects like hyperkalemia (high potassium) and worsening kidney function without improving cardiovascular outcomes.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which strains the right side of the heart.

In the early stages, PAH may cause no noticeable symptoms. As it progresses, signs often mimic other heart or lung conditions:

Chest pain or pressure.
Dizziness or lightheadedness.
Heart palpitations or a rapid, pounding heartbeat.

As the right side of the heart becomes overworked or begins to fail, more severe signs can appear:
Swelling (edema) in the ankles, legs, feet, or abdomen.
Fainting spells (syncope), particularly during or after exertion.
Blue or gray-tinted lips and skin (cyanosis) due to low oxygen levels.

Headache (reported in about 14% of patients)

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over several years, and many people have subtle or no early symptoms.
Early Warning Signs
Frequent urination (polyuria): Needing to pee more often—especially at night—happens as your kidneys try to flush out extra blood sugar.
Increased thirst (polydipsia): Dehydration from frequent urination triggers an intense, constant need to drink.
Persistent fatigue: When your cells cannot properly absorb glucose for energy, you feel unusually tired even with adequate rest.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar causes fluid shifts that can swell the lenses of your eyes.
Increased hunger (polyphagia): Your body fails to use blood sugar for fuel properly, leaving you feeling hungry shortly after eating.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: High blood sugar impairs circulation and weakens the immune response, making minor wounds take much longer to heal.
Frequent infections: Recurring urinary tract infections (UTIs) or yeast infections happen because excess sugar in fluids and tissues encourages bacteria and fungus to grow.
Darkened skin patches: A condition called acanthosis nigricans causes dark, velvety skin folds around the neck, armpits, or groin as a sign of insulin resistance.
Tingling or numbness: Early peripheral nerve damage can cause a mild prickling or loss of sensation in the hands or feet.
How It Is Diagnosed
Doctors confirm Type 2 diabetes using simple blood tests through the Cleveland Clinic or your primary care provider:
Fasting plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar after an 8-hour fast; 126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.
A1C test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months; 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes.
Random plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar at any time; 200 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes (often paired with symptoms).

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure blood sugar or average glucose levels over time.
Diagnostic Criteria
According to guidelines from the American Diabetes Association, type 2 diabetes is diagnosed when any of the following thresholds are met:
Hemoglobin A1C Test: ≥ 6.5% (measures average blood sugar over the past 3 months)
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) after fasting for at least 8 hours
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) at the 2-hour mark after drinking a 75-gram glucose solution
Random Plasma Glucose Test: ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) in a person experiencing classic symptoms of high blood sugar (such as frequent urination, excessive thirst, or unexplained weight loss)
Unless symptoms of severe hyperglycemia are present, doctors typically require a second confirmation test—either repeating the same test or using a different test—to officially confirm the diagnosis.
Screening Recommendations
Routine screening for type 2 diabetes is recommended for:
Adults aged 35 and older
Younger adults and children with risk factors such as overweight or obesity, a family history of diabetes, physical inactivity, or high-risk racial/ethnic backgrounds
Learn more about testing and early indicators through the CDC Diabetes Testing Guide.
