Treatment options for type 2 diabetes focus on lowering blood glucose levels, managing weight, and preventing long-term complications.
1. Lifestyle Modifications
Diet: Eat nutrient-dense, fiber-rich foods like non-starchy vegetables, lean proteins, and healthy fats (such as the Mediterranean or DASH diet).
Physical Activity: Get regular exercise, such as brisk walking, to help your body use insulin more effectively.
Weight Management: Losing even 5% to 7% of your body weight can significantly improve blood sugar regulation.
2. Oral Medications
Metformin: Often prescribed as the first-line medication. It lowers glucose production in the liver and helps muscle cells respond better to insulin.
Sulfonylureas: (e.g., glipizide, glimepiride) Stimulate the pancreas to produce more insulin.
DPP-4 Inhibitors: (Gliptins) Help block the breakdown of hormones that trigger insulin release after meals.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: Help the kidneys remove excess glucose from the body through urine.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): Improve insulin sensitivity in muscle, fat, and liver cells.
Meglitinides: Stimulate fast insulin release around mealtimes.
3. Injectable Medications
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists & Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonists: Injectable drugs that boost insulin secretion, slow digestion, and frequently support weight loss.
Insulin Therapy: Used when oral or non-insulin injectables are no longer enough, or if blood sugar is severely elevated at diagnosis. Options range from long-acting baseline insulins to rapid-acting mealtime insulins.
4. Surgical & Monitoring Options
Weight-Loss (Bariatric) Surgery: Can significantly alter metabolic function and drive type 2 diabetes into remission for eligible patients with obesity.
Blood Sugar Tracking: Use traditional home blood glucose meters or a Continuous Glucose Monitor (CGM) to track real-time levels.

Jardiance (empagliflozin) can cause a range of common and serious side effects because it works by helping your kidneys flush extra sugar and fluid out of your body through your urine.
Common Side Effects
Urinary tract infections (UTIs): Symptoms include a burning sensation when you pee, urinating more frequently in small amounts, or cloudy/bloody urine.
Genital yeast infections: Vaginal yeast infections are common in women (causing thick white discharge, itching, or burning), and fungal or yeast infections can also affect the penis or scrotum in men.
Increased urination: You will likely need to pee more often or in larger amounts, as the drug removes excess glucose.
Increased thirst and dehydration: Losing extra fluid can lead to feeling thirsty, lightheaded, dizzy, or weak—especially when standing up.
Serious Side Effects
Seek emergency medical attention or contact your prescriber right away if you experience signs of these severe conditions:
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): A dangerous buildup of acid in the blood (which can happen even if your blood sugar is not very high). Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach-area pain, unusual fatigue, sweet- or fruity-smelling breath, and trouble breathing.
Necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier's gangrene): A rare but life-threatening bacterial infection of the tissue under the skin in the perineum (area between the genitals and the anus), marked by fever, malaise, severe pain, redness, or swelling in that region.
Severe urinary tract or kidney infections: Such as pyelonephritis (kidney infection) or urosepsis, presenting with high fever, chills, and lower back or flank pain.
Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar): Most common if Jardiance is taken alongside other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas. Signs include shakiness, fast heartbeat, confusion, sweating, and extreme hunger.
Lower limb amputations: Reports show an increased risk of leg or foot amputations, so you should monitor for new sores, pain, tenderness, or ulcers on your feet.
Serious allergic reactions: Symptoms include swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, severe hives, or difficulty breathing.

Neither SGLT2 inhibitors nor GLP-1 receptor agonists have completely replaced metformin as the universal first-line drug for type 2 diabetes, according to guidelines from the American College of Cardiology , though clinical selection depends heavily on specific organ protection and patient risk factors.
Core Comparison
Metformin remains the standard initial medication for most patients with type 2 diabetes unless contraindicated.
SGLT2 Inhibitors (oral, e.g., empagliflozin, canagliflozin) are prioritized if the patient has heart failure or chronic kidney disease (CKD) .
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (mostly injectable, e.g., semaglutide, dulaglutide, though oral semaglutide is available) are prioritized for patients at high risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), stroke prevention , or significant weight loss.
Key Clinical Differences
Kidney Protection: SGLT2 inhibitors generally show stronger evidence for slowing CKD progression and reducing end-stage kidney disease.
Weight Loss: GLP-1 receptor agonists typically yield greater weight loss (4 to 6 kg) compared to SGLT2 inhibitors (1 to 3 kg).
Heart Failure: SGLT2 inhibitors explicitly reduce hospitalizations for heart failure.
Route & Convenience: SGLT2 inhibitors are daily oral pills. GLP-1 RAs have traditionally been weekly or daily injections, though oral options exist.
Combination Therapy: Guidelines often recommend combining both classes with metformin if a patient has multiple high-risk conditions.

High blood pressure (hypertension) is often called a "silent killer" because it typically does not cause any symptoms. Most people with high blood pressure feel completely fine and can live with it for years without knowing it.
Symptoms During Dangerously High Levels (Hypertensive Crisis)
Symptoms usually only appear when blood pressure becomes severely elevated (often above 180/120 mm Hg). Seek emergency care immediately if extremely high blood pressure is accompanied by any of these warning signs:
Chest pain
Shortness of breath
Sudden vision changes (such as blurred or double vision)
Severe headaches
Confusion, dizziness, or neurological changes (such as numbness, weakness, or difficulty speaking)
Back pain
Subtle or Less Common Signs
In some cases, people with elevated or rising blood pressure may occasionally notice mild or subtle signs, though these are not always reliable indicators of hypertension:
Fatigue or feeling tired all the time
Blood spots in the eyes (subconjunctival hemorrhage)
Dizziness or lightheadedness
Recurrent nosebleeds
Headaches, particularly early in the morning
How to Know Your Numbers
Because symptoms are rare, checking your blood pressure regularly is the only way to detect hypertension. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the American Heart Association recommend routine checks at least once a year if you are an adult, or as advised by your healthcare provider. You can also review detailed blood pressure categories and guidelines on the Mayo Clinic High Blood Pressure Overview.

High blood pressure (hypertension) is generally defined as a consistent reading of 130/80 mm Hg or higher.
Blood pressure is measured using two numbers:
Systolic (top number): The pressure in your arteries when your heart contracts.
Diastolic (bottom number): The pressure in your arteries when your heart relaxes between beats.
According to guidelines from the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, blood pressure categories are broken down as follows:
Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 1 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 130–139 mm Hg systolic or 80–89 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 2 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 140 mm Hg or higher systolic or 90 mm Hg or higher diastolic
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic
What the Stages Mean
Elevated blood pressure is a warning sign that you are at risk of developing full hypertension unless you take steps to improve your habits.
Stage 1 hypertension typically leads a healthcare provider to recommend lifestyle modifications, and potentially medication if you have a high risk of heart disease or stroke.
Stage 2 hypertension usually requires a combination of prescribed blood pressure medications and lifestyle changes.
A reading over 180/120 mm Hg is a medical emergency. If your reading is this high, wait five minutes and test again. If it remains this high and you have symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, or vision changes, call 911 immediately. If you don't have symptoms, contact your doctor right away.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is typically managed through a combination of lifestyle changes, prescription medications, and—in specific cases—specialized medical procedures.
1. Lifestyle Modifications
Heart-healthy habits form the foundation of treatment and can improve the effectiveness of medications:
Dietary Changes: Follow the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) eating plan, which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fats.
Sodium Reduction: Lower salt and sodium intake (aiming for less than 2,000 mg per day) to help drop blood pressure.
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise (such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming) and resistance training.
Weight Management: Achieve and maintain a healthy body weight.
Limit Alcohol and Avoid Tobacco: Reduce or stop alcohol consumption and quit smoking.
2. Medication Options (Antihypertensives)
When lifestyle changes are not enough, doctors frequently prescribe one or more classes of blood pressure medications. Common first-line drug classes include:
ACE Inhibitors (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors): Relax and widen blood vessels (e.g., lisinopril, ramipril).
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): Block the action of chemicals that narrow blood vessels (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers: Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells to allow vessels to relax (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the body flush out excess sodium and water, reducing fluid volume (e.g., thiazides like hydrochlorothiazide).
Other Medications: Depending on individual health needs or coexisting conditions (like heart disease or kidney issues), providers may use beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, or central-acting agents. Many patients require a combination of two or more drugs.
3. Procedures for Resistant Hypertension
Renal Denervation: A minimally invasive procedure that uses energy pulses to calm overactive nerves near the kidneys for patients whose blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite lifestyle changes and multiple medications.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) are both effective first-line medications for high blood pressure (hypertension), providing similar reductions in blood pressure and protection against major cardiovascular events, though ARBs are generally better tolerated.
Efficacy and Comparison
Blood Pressure Control: Both classes lower blood pressure equally well by inhibiting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), which relaxes and widens blood vessels.
Hard Outcomes: Large clinical analyses show little to no difference between ACE inhibitors and ARBs regarding overall mortality, heart attacks, strokes, or kidney disease progression.
Guidelines: Major organizations—such as the American College of Cardiology (ACC), American Heart Association (AHA), and European Society of Cardiology (ESC)—historically listed ACE inhibitors and ARBs as co-equal first-line options (alongside calcium channel blockers and thiazide diuretics). However, recent real-world data and guidelines increasingly favor ARBs due to a more favorable safety profile .
Key Differences and Side Effects
Cough: A persistent, dry cough is a well-known side effect of ACE inhibitors (caused by the buildup of bradykinin). This side effect does not occur with ARBs.
Angioedema: Both classes carry a rare risk of angioedema (severe tissue swelling, particularly of the face or throat), though the risk is significantly lower with ARBs.
Adherence/Withdrawal: Because ARBs cause fewer annoying side effects like cough, patient discontinuation and treatment withdrawal rates are lower compared to ACE inhibitors.
Combination Therapy: You should never take an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together. Dual blockade does not improve outcomes and dramatically increases the risk of side effects like low blood pressure, high potassium (hyperkalemia), and kidney damage .

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over months or years, and many people have few or no noticeable signs in the early stages.
Early Warning Signs
Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar pulls fluid out of your tissues, making you feel thirstier than usual and leading to more frequent bathroom visits, especially at night.
Persistent fatigue: When your cells cannot properly absorb glucose (sugar) from your blood to use for energy, you can feel unusually tired or run-down.
Blurred vision: Excess sugar in the blood can cause fluid to shift into the lenses of your eyes, leading to temporary swelling and blurry sight.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: High blood sugar damages blood vessels and impairs circulation, slowing down your body's natural healing process.
Frequent infections: Elevated glucose levels can weaken the immune system, leading to more frequent skin, gum, or urinary tract infections.
Tingling or numbness: Peripheral nerve damage (neuropathy) from chronic high blood sugar often starts as a prickling, numbness, or burning sensation in the hands or feet.
Darkened skin patches: A condition called acanthosis nigricans causes dark, velvety skin folds—most commonly around the neck, armpits, or groin—and is a visual sign of insulin resistance.
Unexplained weight changes: While some people experience sudden weight loss because the body starts burning muscle and fat for energy, others may experience weight gain or increased hunger.
How It Is Diagnosed
If you notice any of these symptoms or have risk factors like a family history or age over 45, a healthcare provider can check your blood sugar using standard diagnostic tests detailed by the Cleveland Clinic:
Fasting plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar after an 8-hour fast (126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes).
A1C test: Measures average blood sugar levels over the past 2 to 3 months (6.5% or higher indicates diabetes).
Random plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar at any time without fasting (200 mg/dL or higher with symptoms indicates diabetes).

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests ordered by a doctor to measure blood sugar levels. Unless a person has clear symptoms of high blood sugar, doctors typically repeat the test on a second day to confirm the diagnosis.
Key Blood Tests for Diagnosis
Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) Test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months.
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: Measures your blood sugar after you have had nothing to eat or drink (except water) for at least 8 hours.
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): Measures your blood sugar before and 2 hours after you drink a special sugary liquid (after an 8-hour fast).
Random Plasma Glucose Test: Measures your blood sugar at any time of day, regardless of when you last ate.
Screening Recommendations
Major health organizations (such as the American Diabetes Association) recommend routine screening for Type 2 diabetes:
Adults aged 35 and older
Adults of any age who are overweight or obese and have additional risk factors (such as a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure, or a history of gestational diabetes).
You can learn more about managing risk factors and guidance on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention .

Treatment options for type 2 diabetes focus on lowering blood glucose levels, managing weight, and preventing long-term complications.
1. Lifestyle Modifications
Diet: Eat nutrient-dense, fiber-rich foods like non-starchy vegetables, lean proteins, and healthy fats (such as the Mediterranean or DASH diet).
Physical Activity: Get regular exercise, such as brisk walking, to help your body use insulin more effectively.
Weight Management: Losing even 5% to 7% of your body weight can significantly improve blood sugar regulation.
2. Oral Medications
Metformin: Often prescribed as the first-line medication. It lowers glucose production in the liver and helps muscle cells respond better to insulin.
Sulfonylureas: (e.g., glipizide, glimepiride) Stimulate the pancreas to produce more insulin.
DPP-4 Inhibitors: (Gliptins) Help block the breakdown of hormones that trigger insulin release after meals.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: Help the kidneys remove excess glucose from the body through urine.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): Improve insulin sensitivity in muscle, fat, and liver cells.
Meglitinides: Stimulate fast insulin release around mealtimes.
3. Injectable Medications
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists & Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonists: Injectable drugs that boost insulin secretion, slow digestion, and frequently support weight loss.
Insulin Therapy: Used when oral or non-insulin injectables are no longer enough, or if blood sugar is severely elevated at diagnosis. Options range from long-acting baseline insulins to rapid-acting mealtime insulins.
4. Surgical & Monitoring Options
Weight-Loss (Bariatric) Surgery: Can significantly alter metabolic function and drive type 2 diabetes into remission for eligible patients with obesity.
Blood Sugar Tracking: Use traditional home blood glucose meters or a Continuous Glucose Monitor (CGM) to track real-time levels.
For more information on medications and management strategies, review the Mayo Clinic Guide to Type 2 Diabetes or the Cleveland Clinic Diabetes Overview.

Common and serious side effects associated with Jardiance (empagliflozin) are tied to how the medication works by helping the kidneys remove extra sugar and fluid through urine.
Common Side Effects
Urinary tract infections (UTIs): Burning, urgency, frequency, pain, or cloudy urine.
Genital yeast infections: Vaginal yeast infections (itching, burning, thick white discharge) in women, or yeast infections around the penis and scrotum in men.
Increased urination: Going to the bathroom more often or needing to pee more frequently during the day or night.
Increased thirst: Dry mouth or a greater need to drink fluids.
Serious Side Effects
Seek immediate medical attention or contact your healthcare provider right away if you experience signs of these severe reactions:
Dehydration: Dizziness, lightheadedness, feeling faint, weakness, or dark yellow urine—especially if you are older, take water pills (diuretics), or have kidney issues.
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): A dangerous buildup of acid in the blood, which can happen even if blood sugar is not very high. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, unusual fatigue, trouble breathing, or a fruity odor on your breath.
Low blood sugar (Hypoglycemia): More common if Jardiance is taken alongside other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas. Symptoms include shakiness, confusion, fast heart rate, and cold sweats.
Severe urinary tract or kidney infections: High fever, chills, lower back or side pain.
Necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier's gangrene): A rare, life-threatening bacterial infection of the tissue under the skin in the perineal (genital and rectal) area, causing severe pain, redness, swelling, and fever.
Lower limb amputations: Higher risk reported in patients with a history of amputation, peripheral vascular disease, or diabetic foot ulcers.
Serious allergic reactions: Hives, or swelling of the face, lips, tongue, and throat causing difficulty breathing or swallowing.

High blood pressure (hypertension) is often called a "silent killer" because it typically causes no signs or symptoms. Most people with high blood pressure feel completely normal and do not realize their numbers are high.
You can check your current categories through the American Heart Association or learn more from the CDC High Blood Pressure Overview.
When Symptoms Do Appear (Dangerously High or Rising Blood Pressure)
While rare during normal hypertension, severely elevated blood pressure or a rapid spike can sometimes trigger physical signs:
Severe headaches
Dizziness or lightheadedness
Fatigue or feeling exhausted all the time
Vision changes (such as blurred vision or dark spots)
Blood spots in the eyes (broken tiny blood vessels)
Shortness of breath
Hypertensive Emergency Warning Signs (Call 911)
If a blood pressure reading is higher than 180/120 mm Hg, wait one minute and re-test. If the second reading remains above 180/120 mm Hg and is accompanied by any of the following emergency symptoms, call 911 immediately:
Chest pain or back pain
Shortness of breath
Sudden weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking
Sudden confusion
Severe change in vision
(If your reading is above 180/120 mm Hg but you do not have these symptoms, contact your doctor right away for guidance).
How to Know Your Numbers
Because symptoms are rarely reliable, the only way to know if you have high blood pressure is to measure it regularly with a blood pressure cuff at a doctor’s office or at home.

Blood pressure is measured using two numbers: systolic (top number) and diastolic (bottom number), recorded in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg). According to guidelines from the American Heart Association , blood pressure categories are defined as follows:
Normal: Less than 120 / less than 80 mm Hg
Elevated: 120–129 / less than 80 mm Hg
Stage 1 High Blood Pressure (Hypertension): 130–139 / 80–89 mm Hg
Stage 2 High Blood Pressure (Hypertension): 140 or higher / 90 or higher mm Hg
Hypertensive Crisis (Medical Emergency): Higher than 180 / higher than 120 mm Hg
What the Numbers Mean
Systolic (Top Number): Measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart contracts.
Diastolic (Bottom Number): Measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart rests between beats.
High Diagnosis: High blood pressure is diagnosed if either the top or bottom number consistently falls into an elevated or hypertensive range .
What to Do in a Crisis
If your blood pressure reading exceeds 180/120 mm Hg, wait five minutes and retest. If your numbers are still that high and you have warning signs like chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, or trouble speaking, call 911 immediately.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is typically managed through a combination of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications.
1. Lifestyle Modifications
Lifestyle changes are recommended for everyone with high blood pressure and can sometimes reduce the need for or dosage of medications:
Dietary Approaches: Adopt the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) eating plan, which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fats.
Sodium Reduction: Lower daily salt and sodium intake (ideally aiming for under 1,500 to 2,000 mg per day).
Regular Exercise: Engage in regular aerobic activity, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming, for at least 30 minutes most days.
Weight Management: Lose extra weight if you are overweight or obese to decrease the strain on your heart and blood vessels.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce alcohol consumption and stop smoking or using tobacco products, which constrict blood vessels and raise heart rates.
Stress Management: Practice relaxation or stress-reduction techniques and aim for 7 to 8 hours of quality sleep per night.
2. Pharmacologic Therapy (Medications)
If lifestyle changes alone do not lower your blood pressure to your target goal (generally less than 130/80 mm Hg for most adults), your doctor may prescribe one or more medications.
The primary first-line classes of blood pressure medications include:
Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors: Keep blood vessels from narrowing by blocking the formation of a natural chemical that tightens them (e.g., lisinopril, benazepril).
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Relax blood vessels by blocking the action—rather than the formation—of that same narrowing chemical (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering the muscle cells of your heart and blood vessels, allowing the vessels to relax and widen (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Thiazide Diuretics: Often called "water pills," these help your kidneys remove excess sodium and water from your body, lowering blood volume (e.g., chlorthalidone, hydrochlorothiazide).
Additional or Second-Line Options
Beta-Blockers: Lower the heart rate and the heart's output of blood; often prescribed if you also have coronary artery disease or heart failure.
Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists & Vasodilators: Sometimes added if blood pressure remains high despite multi-drug treatment (resistant hypertension).
Note: Many people require a combination of two or more blood pressure drugs—sometimes available in a single, fixed-dose pill—to reach their target safely.
Resources for Guidance
You can explore official educational tools and treatment navigators through the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), review medication categories with the American Heart Association, or track guidelines via the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Losartan is a prescription medication used to treat high blood pressure, protect the kidneys in type 2 diabetes, and lower the risk of stroke. While generally well-tolerated, it can cause several side effects.
Common Side Effects
Most common side effects are mild and tend to improve as your body adjusts to the medication:
Dizziness or lightheadedness (especially when standing up quickly)
Upper respiratory symptoms (such as a stuffy or runny nose, sore throat, or cold-like symptoms)
Fatigue or tiredness
Back, leg, or joint pain
Headache
Digestive issues (such as nausea, diarrhea, or mild stomach upset)
Serious Side Effects
Seek immediate medical attention or contact your healthcare provider right away if you experience:
Allergic reactions (anaphylaxis): Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat, or eyes, or severe difficulty breathing or swallowing.
High potassium levels (hyperkalemia): Muscle weakness, confusion, or a fast or irregular heartbeat.
Kidney problems: A sudden decrease in urination or swelling in your hands, ankles, or feet.
Very low blood pressure (hypotension): Fainting, severe lightheadedness, or extreme wooziness.
Chest pain.
Liver problems: Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice) or severe upper stomach pain.
Important Safety Notes
Pregnancy Warning: Losartan should not be taken during pregnancy as it can cause serious injury or death to an unborn baby.
Interactions: Avoid starting potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes, or NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or naproxen) without talking to your doctor, as they can interact with losartan or worsen kidney and potassium levels.
Consult a Doctor: Review official details on the Mayo Clinic Losartan Guide or speak with your pharmacist or doctor before making any changes to your medication.

Both ACE inhibitors (ending in -pril, such as lisinopril) and ARBs (ending in -sartan , such as losartan) are equally recommended as Class I first-line options for treating primary hypertension.
Large-scale real-world studies (such as the LEGEND-HTN network study) and clinical trials show that both drug classes lower blood pressure and offer comparable cardiovascular effectiveness (no significant difference in heart attack, stroke, or heart failure risk). However, they differ in how they work and their side-effect profiles:
Mechanism of Action
ACE Inhibitors: Block the enzyme that converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II (a potent vasoconstrictor). They also cause a buildup of bradykinin, which can trigger side effects .
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): Block angiotensin II directly from binding to its cellular receptors (AT1 receptors) without affecting bradykinin levels.
Side Effects and Tolerability
ACE Inhibitors: Have a higher rate of adverse effects, most notably a persistent dry, scratchy cough (~10% of patients) and a risk of serious or life-threatening facial/throat swelling ().
ARBs: Have a significantly better safety and tolerability profile. They carry a much lower risk of dry cough (~3%) and rare angioedema, making them the preferred alternative or first-line pick for patients sensitive to ACE inhibitors.
Shared Precautions
Pregnancy: Both classes are strictly contraindicated during pregnancy (teratogenic/harmful to the fetus).
Kidney & Electrolyte Risks: Both can cause elevated potassium levels (hyperkalemia) or acute changes in kidney function, and they should never be combined with each other .
Current clinical evidence leans toward preferentially starting with an ARB over an ACE inhibitor due to better patient adherence and fewer bothersome or dangerous side effects, though individual choice depends on medical history, insurance/cost, and provider preference. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, making the right side of the heart work too hard to pump blood.
Early and Common Symptoms
In the early stages, PAH may cause no symptoms or mimic other common lung and heart conditions. As the blood vessels in the lungs thicken and narrow, common signs include:
Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially during physical exertion or climbing stairs
Extreme fatigue and general weakness
Chest pain or pressure
Dizziness or lightheadedness
Heart palpitations or a fast, racing heartbeat
Progressive and Advanced Symptoms
As the strain on the right side of the heart increases and right-sided heart failure develops, additional symptoms often appear:
Swelling (edema) in the ankles, legs, or feet
Swollen abdomen (ascites or fluid retention) from blood backing up toward the liver and kidneys
Fainting spells (syncope), particularly during or after physical activity
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) in severe cases
Hoarseness caused by an enlarged pulmonary artery pressing on chest nerves
You can learn more about recognizing warning signs and diagnostic testing via the American Lung Association or review broader risk details from the Mayo Clinic.

Opsumit (macitentan) is a prescription medication used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). It can cause both common and serious side effects.
Common Side Effects
Headache
Nasopharyngitis (common cold or stuffy nose)
Bronchitis or upper respiratory tract infections
Anemia (low red blood cell count)
Urinary tract infection (UTI)
Influenza (flu-like symptoms)
Serious Side Effects
Severe Birth Defects: Opsumit causes major harm to an unborn baby if taken during pregnancy. Females of childbearing potential must have negative pregnancy tests and use effective contraception.
Liver Damage: It can affect liver function. Your doctor will check your liver with blood tests before you start and during treatment. Signs of liver issues include nausea, vomiting, upper right stomach pain, fatigue, loss of appetite, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin/eyes.
Fluid Retention and Edema: Swelling in the hands, legs, or feet, or rapid weight gain can happen, especially during the first weeks of treatment.
Low Red Blood Cell Levels (Anemia): Significant drops in hemoglobin can occur, sometimes requiring a blood transfusion.
Decreased Sperm Counts: Opsumit may reduce sperm counts and impact male fertility.

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over many months or years, and many people have mild or no symptoms in the early stages. When early signs do appear, they are usually subtle and easy to miss.
Common Early Signs and Symptoms
Increased Thirst (Polydipsia): You feel unusually thirsty even after drinking water, because high blood sugar pulls fluid out of your tissues.
Frequent Urination (Polyuria): You need to pee more often, especially at night, as your kidneys work overtime to filter and flush out the extra glucose.
Persistent Fatigue: You feel constantly tired or drained because your body's cells cannot properly absorb and use glucose for energy.
Increased Hunger: You feel hungry shortly after eating because your cells are starved for the energy they cannot process.
Blurred Vision: High blood sugar causes fluid to shift into the lenses of your eyes, making it hard to focus.
Slow-Healing Sores or Cuts: Cuts, scrapes, or minor bruises take a long time to heal due to poor circulation and a weakened immune response.
Frequent Infections: You experience recurring skin infections, gum disease, or urinary tract infections (UTIs) because excess sugar feeds bacteria and yeast.
Numbness or Tingling: You feel a prickling, numbness, or burning sensation in your hands or feet (peripheral neuropathy).
Darkened Skin Patches: You notice dark, velvety patches of skin (called acanthosis nigricans), most commonly around your neck, armpits, or groin, which is a sign of insulin resistance.
Unexplained Weight Changes: You might experience unexpected weight loss (as the body burns muscle and fat for fuel) or subtle weight gain around the abdomen.
How Type 2 Diabetes Is Diagnosed
Because symptoms can be so quiet, doctors rely on simple blood tests to confirm if you have type 2 diabetes or prediabetes:
Fasting Plasma Glucose Test: Measures blood sugar after an 8-hour fast; a result of 126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.
A1C Test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months; a result of 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes.
Random Plasma Glucose Test: Measures blood sugar at any time without fasting; a result of 200 mg/dL or higher points to diabetes.
You can learn more about symptoms and diagnostic standards through the Mayo Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Guide or the Cleveland Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Overview.

GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (e.g., semaglutide, dulaglutide)

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is typically managed through a combination of heart-healthy lifestyle modifications and prescription medications.
Lifestyle Modifications
Lifestyle changes are recommended for everyone with elevated blood pressure or hypertension:
Dietary Changes: Adopt the DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension), which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products.
Sodium Reduction: Lower salt intake (ideally aiming for less than 2,000 mg per day).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming.
Weight and Alcohol Management: Lose excess body weight if needed and limit alcohol consumption.
First-Line Medications
When lifestyle changes are not enough—or immediately for higher blood pressure or elevated cardiovascular risk—doctors prescribe antihypertensive drugs. The four primary classes of first-line medications include:
Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors: Relax blood vessels by preventing the body from producing a hormone that narrows them (e.g., lisinopril).
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Block the action of blood-vessel-constricting hormones to keep vessels open (e.g., losartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells, allowing vessels to relax and widen (e.g., amlodipine).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the kidneys remove excess sodium and water from the body, lowering fluid volume (e.g., thiazide diuretics).
Additional and Advanced Options
Combination Therapy: Many people need two or more blood pressure medications (often in a single combination pill) to reach their target goal—typically less than 130/80 mm Hg.
Other Classes: Depending on other health conditions (like heart failure or kidney disease), doctors may add beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, or central-acting agents.
Resistant Hypertension: If blood pressure remains high despite taking three or more drugs (including a diuretic), specialists may evaluate for underlying causes, adjust regimens, or consider specialized procedures like renal denervation.

Common and serious side effects of losartan (Cozaar) include:
Common or Mild Side Effects
Dizziness or lightheadedness (especially when standing up quickly)
Fatigue or weakness
Headache (often temporary during the first 1 to 2 weeks)
Upper respiratory tract infections or stuffy nose
Back, joint, or muscle pain / cramps
Digestive upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or mild stomach pain)
Serious Side Effects (Seek Immediate Medical Attention)
Angioedema: Severe swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat, eyes, or mouth, which can cause difficulty breathing or swallowing.
High potassium levels (Hyperkalemia): Symptoms include muscle weakness, confusion, shortness of breath, or a fast/irregular heartbeat.
Kidney problems or injury: Signs include a decrease in the amount of urine produced, blood in the urine, or sudden swelling in the legs, ankles, or feet.
Severely low blood pressure (Hypotension): Causing fainting, severe dizziness, or blurry vision.
Liver problems: Signs include yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice).
Important Precautions
Pregnancy Warning: Losartan must not be taken during pregnancy as it can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby.
Medication Interactions: Use caution or avoid combining losartan with potassium supplements, salt substitutes containing potassium, ACE inhibitors, or NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or naproxen) without talking to your doctor.
Most mild side effects like dizziness and headaches improve over time as your body adjusts to the medication.

Both angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are recommended as first-line therapy for high blood pressure (hypertension).
Effectiveness: Large-scale studies show that ACE inhibitors (such as lisinopril) and ARBs (such as losartan) lower blood pressure and protect the heart and kidneys just as well as each other.
Safety and Side Effects: ARBs generally have a better safety profile with fewer side effects. ACE inhibitors frequently cause a persistent dry cough and carry a risk of angioedema (swelling of the face or throat) due to bradykinin buildup; these side effects are much less common with ARBs .
Current Clinical Preference: Because they provide equal blood pressure control with fewer adverse events, many modern clinical evaluations and health networks suggest preferentially starting with an ARB over an ACE inhibitor. If a patient cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor due to a cough or side effects, switching to an ARB is the standard approach .

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which strains the right side of the heart.
Early and Common Symptoms
In the early stages, PAH often causes no symptoms or mimics other heart and lung conditions. As it progresses, the most frequent signs include:
Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially during physical activity or exertion
Fatigue and unusual tiredness during daily tasks
Chest pain, pressure, or discomfort resulting from an overworked heart
Dizziness or lightheadedness, particularly when moving or exerting yourself
Heart palpitations (a racing or pounding heartbeat)
Progressive and Advanced Symptoms
As right-sided heart strain or failure develops, more pronounced physical signs may appear:
Swelling (edema) in the ankles, feet, legs, or abdomen due to fluid retention
Fainting spells (syncope) triggered by reduced oxygen flow to the brain
Bluish lips or skin (cyanosis) caused by low blood oxygen levels
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or hoarseness from an enlarged artery pressing on chest nerves in rare, severe cases

Opsumit (macitentan) is a prescription medication used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). It can cause both common and serious side effects.
Common Side Effects
Headache

Bronchitis or upper respiratory tract infections
Anemia (low red blood cell count)
Urinary tract infection (UTI)
Influenza (flu-like symptoms)
Serious Side Effects
Severe Birth Defects: Opsumit causes major harm to an unborn baby if taken during pregnancy. Females of childbearing potential must have negative pregnancy tests and use effective contraception.
Liver Damage: It can affect liver function. Your doctor will check your liver with blood tests before you start and during treatment. Signs of liver issues include nausea, vomiting, upper right stomach pain, fatigue, loss of appetite, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin/eyes.

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over years, and many people do not notice any early symptoms at all.
Common Early Signs and Symptoms
Increased Thirst and Frequent Urination: Excess sugar (glucose) builds up in your blood, forcing your kidneys to work overtime to filter and absorb it. When they cannot keep up, the excess sugar is excreted into your urine, pulling fluids from your tissues and causing you to pee more often—especially at night—and feel constantly thirsty.
Fatigue and Weakness: Even though there is plenty of sugar in your bloodstream, it cannot enter your cells properly to be used for energy because of insulin resistance. This leaves you feeling unusually tired or drained.
Blurred Vision: High blood sugar levels can cause fluid to shift into the lenses of your eyes, changing their shape and making it difficult to focus.
Slow-Healing Sores or Wounds: Poor circulation and damage to blood vessels from high blood sugar make it harder for your body to repair cuts, bruises, or sores.
Frequent Infections: High glucose levels create an environment where bacteria and yeast can thrive, leading to recurring skin, gum, or urinary tract infections.
Tingling or Numbness: High blood sugar over time can damage your nerves (peripheral neuropathy), often starting as a pins-and-needles sensation or numbness in your hands or feet.
Unexplained Weight Loss or Gain: Your body may start burning fat and muscle for energy if it cannot use glucose properly (leading to sudden weight loss), or you may experience weight gain linked to underlying insulin resistance.
Darkened Patches of Skin (Acanthosis Nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin can develop in body folds and creases—most commonly around the neck, armpits, or groin—as a sign of insulin resistance.
Screening and Diagnosis
Because symptoms are subtle or absent, the Cleveland Clinic or your primary care provider can check for type 2 diabetes using routine blood tests:
A1C Test: Measures your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months (6.5% or higher indicates diabetes).
Fasting Plasma Glucose Test: Measures your blood sugar after an 8-hour fast (126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes).
Random Plasma Glucose Test: Taken at any time without fasting (200 mg/dL or higher, accompanied by symptoms, indicates diabetes).

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests performed in a clinical or laboratory setting. In most cases without severe symptoms, the test must be repeated on a second day to confirm the diagnosis.
Key Diagnostic Blood Tests
Hemoglobin A1C Test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months.
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: Measures your blood sugar after fasting (no food or drink except water) for at least 8 hours.
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): Measures your blood sugar before and 2 hours after you drink a special sweet glucose liquid (after an 8-hour fast).
Random Plasma Glucose Test: Measures your blood sugar at any time of day, regardless of when you last ate.
Confirmation and Screening Guidelines
Repeat Testing: If you do not have clear, classic symptoms of high blood sugar, doctors generally require a repeat test (using the same or a different test) on a separate day to confirm a type 2 diabetes diagnosis. If you have severe symptoms and a very high blood sugar reading, a single test may be enough .
Routine Screening: The American Diabetes Association recommends routine screening for all adults starting at age 35, or earlier if you have risk factors such as overweight/obesity, a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure, or a history of gestational diabetes.
More details on testing and criteria can be reviewed through the MedlinePlus Diabetes Type 2 Guide .

Treatment options for type 2 diabetes include lifestyle changes, oral and injectable medications, insulin therapy, and surgical options to help manage blood sugar levels and prevent complications.
Lifestyle Modifications
Healthy Diet: Focus on whole foods, lean proteins, non-starchy vegetables, complex carbohydrates, and healthy fats while managing portion sizes.
Physical Activity: Incorporate regular cardiovascular exercise combined with strength training.
Weight Management: Working toward achieving a healthy body weight can significantly improve insulin sensitivity.
Oral Medications
Metformin: Often the first-line medication prescribed; it works by reducing glucose production in the liver and helping the body use insulin more effectively.
Sulfonylureas: Medications like glipizide or glimepiride help the pancreas release more insulin.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): Drugs like pioglitazone help improve insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat cells.
DPP-4 Inhibitors (Gliptins): Help block enzymes that break down gut hormones, leading to increased insulin production after meals.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: Help the kidneys remove excess glucose from the body through urine.
Injectable Medications
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists & Dual GLP-1/GIP Agonists: Injectable treatments that stimulate insulin release, slow digestion, and frequently assist with weight management and heart or kidney health.
Insulin Therapy: Long-acting, short-acting, or mixed insulins can be prescribed via pens, syringes, or pumps if oral and injectable medications no longer keep blood sugar in a healthy range.
Surgical Interventions
Bariatric Surgery: Can be considered to significantly reduce stomach capacity and improve or reverse type 2 diabetes symptoms.

Jardiance (empagliflozin) can cause common mild side effects as well as rare, serious medical conditions.
Common Side Effects
Increased urination: Urinating more often or in larger amounts because the kidneys remove extra sugar through urine.
Urinary tract infections (UTIs): Symptoms include a burning sensation when you pee, a strong or urgent need to urinate, or cloudy/discolored urine.
Genital yeast infections: Fungal infections can happen around the vagina (itching, thick white discharge, burning) or around the penis and scrotum (redness, rash, irritation).
Increased thirst and mild dehydration: Feeling lightheaded, dizzy, or weak when standing up.
Serious Side Effects
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): A dangerous buildup of acid and ketones in the blood. This can happen even if your blood sugar is not very high. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, unusual tiredness, and trouble breathing.
Severe dehydration and kidney problems: A sharp drop in body water and salt that can lead to sudden worsening of kidney function or low blood pressure.
Necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier’s gangrene): A rare but life-threatening bacterial infection of the tissue under the skin in the perineum (area between the anus and genitals) causing intense pain, swelling, redness, and fever.
Hypoglycemia (Low blood sugar): More likely if you take Jardiance along with other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas. Symptoms include shakiness, cold sweats, confusion, and a fast heartbeat.
Lower limb amputations: An increased risk of leg or foot sores, ulcers, or amputations, particularly if you have a history of vascular disease or previous foot ulcers.
Serious allergic reactions: Hives or swelling of the face, lips, and throat.

High blood pressure (hypertension) is often called the "silent killer" because it typically causes no signs or symptoms. A person can have high blood pressure for years without realizing it while it quietly damages the heart, brain, and kidneys.
The only reliable way to know if you have high blood pressure is to have it measured by a healthcare provider or with a validated home monitor.
When Symptoms Do Appear (Dangerously High Blood Pressure)
Symptoms generally only show up if blood pressure becomes extremely high—a condition known as severe hypertension or a hypertensive crisis (readings above 180/120 mm Hg).
Potential warning signs during severe spikes include:
Severe headaches
Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Chest pain or pressure
Vision changes (such as blurred or double vision)
Dizziness, confusion, or lightheadedness
Numbness or weakness
Difficulty speaking
Nosebleeds
Blood spots in the eyes
Fatigue or feeling exhausted from the heart working harder
What to Do If Blood Pressure Is Very High (>180/120 mm Hg)
Wait 1 minute and retest: If your reading is 180/120 mm Hg or higher, rest for a minute and check it a second time.
If you have symptoms: Call 911 immediately if a reading above 180/120 mm Hg is accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, vision changes, or trouble speaking (signs of a hypertensive emergency).
If you do not have symptoms: Contact your doctor right away for guidance on adjusting or starting medication.

According to guidelines from the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, high blood pressure (hypertension) is diagnosed when your blood pressure readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.
Blood pressure is measured using two numbers: systolic (top number, pressure when the heart beats) and diastolic (bottom number, pressure when the heart rests between beats).
Blood Pressure Categories
Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130–139 mm Hg systolic or 80–89 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140 mm Hg or higher systolic or 90 mm Hg or higher diastolic
Severe Hypertension: Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic (Contact your healthcare professional immediately if you do not have symptoms)
Hypertensive Emergency: Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic accompanied by symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, or confusion (Call 911 immediately)

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is typically managed through a combination of heart-healthy lifestyle modifications and prescription medications.
Lifestyle Modifications
Lifestyle changes are recommended for everyone with elevated blood pressure or hypertension:
Dietary Changes: Adopt the DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension), which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products.
Sodium Reduction: Lower salt intake (ideally aiming for less than 2,000 mg per day).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming.
Weight and Alcohol Management: Lose excess body weight if needed and limit alcohol consumption.
First-Line Medications
When lifestyle changes are not enough—or immediately for higher blood pressure or elevated cardiovascular risk—doctors prescribe antihypertensive drugs. The four primary classes of first-line medications include:
Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors: Relax blood vessels by preventing the body from producing a hormone that narrows them (e.g., lisinopril).
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Block the action of blood-vessel-constricting hormones to keep vessels open (e.g., losartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells, allowing vessels to relax and widen (e.g., amlodipine).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the kidneys remove excess sodium and water from the body, lowering fluid volume (e.g., thiazide diuretics).
Additional and Advanced Options
Combination Therapy: Many people need two or more blood pressure medications (often in a single combination pill) to reach their target goal—typically less than 130/80 mm Hg.
Other Classes: Depending on other health conditions (like heart failure or kidney disease), doctors may add beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, or central-acting agents.
Resistant Hypertension: If blood pressure remains high despite taking three or more drugs (including a diuretic), specialists may evaluate for underlying causes, adjust regimens, or consider specialized procedures like renal denervation.
For more details on treatment guidelines and medication classes, review resources from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute or Mayo Clinic.

Fatigue or weakness
Upper respiratory symptoms (cold-like symptoms, stuffy nose, or sinus pressure)
Back or joint pain
Headache
Digestive issues (mild nausea, diarrhea, or stomach upset)
Dry cough (much less common with losartan than with ACE inhibitors, though still possible in some people)

Both Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs) are effective, guideline-recommended first-line medications for treating high blood pressure, though ARBs are generally preferred today due to a better side-effect profile .
Key Similarities
Blood Pressure Control: Both drug classes lower blood pressure by acting on the body's renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).
Cardiovascular Protection: Large clinical studies and meta-analyses show no significant difference between the two classes in preventing major events like heart attacks, strokes, or heart failure hospitalizations.
Affordability: Generic options for both ACE inhibitors and ARBs are widely available at a low cost.
Key Differences
Mechanism: ACE inhibitors block the enzyme that produces angiotensin II. ARBs block the angiotensin II receptors directly. ACE inhibitors also lead to a buildup of bradykinin, which causes unique side effects.
Side Effects (Cough and Angioedema): ACE inhibitors frequently cause a nagging, dry cough (in up to 10% or more of patients) and carry a higher risk of angioedema (dangerous tissue swelling, particularly of the face or throat). ARBs do not trigger the bradykinin buildup, resulting in a much lower incidence of cough and angioedema.
Adherence: Because ARBs are much better tolerated, patients are less likely to stop taking them compared to ACE inhibitors.
Which Should You Choose?
First-Line Preference: Insights shared via the American Academy of Family Physicians (AFP) and large-scale data reviews discussed on note that while international guidelines traditionally gave both classes equal weight, modern clinical practice leans toward starting with an ARB to avoid side effects.
Switching: If you are already taking an ACE inhibitor and your blood pressure is well-controlled without a cough or other issues, doctors generally do not need to switch you to an ARB. However, if you develop an ACE-inhibitor-induced dry cough, switching to an ARB is a standard and effective solution.
Note: You should never take an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together, as combination therapy increases the risk of high potassium and kidney dysfunction without added cardiovascular benefit.

The primary symptoms of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) result from high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which forces the right side of the heart to work harder and reduces oxygen flow.
Early and Common Symptoms
Shortness of breath (dyspnea): Often the first and most prominent sign, initially occurring during physical exertion (such as climbing stairs or walking) and worsening over time to happen even at rest.
Fatigue and weakness: Persistent tiredness and reduced exercise capacity due to the heart struggling to deliver enough oxygenated blood to the body.
Chest pain or pressure: Discomfort, angina-like pain, or tightness caused by an overworked and strained right heart ventricle.
Dizziness and lightheadedness: Occurs frequently during or after physical activity because of reduced blood flow and oxygen to the brain.
Heart palpitations: A fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat as the heart tries to compensate for the high pressure.
Progressive and Advanced Symptoms
As the condition advances and right-sided heart strain or failure develops, more severe signs appear:
Swelling (edema): Fluid retention leading to swollen ankles, legs, feet, or a bloated/distended abdomen (ascites).
Fainting spells (syncope): Episodes of fainting, particularly during or right after exertion, as blood pressure or oxygen drops sharply.
Cyanosis: A bluish tint to the lips, skin, or fingers caused by low oxygen levels in the blood.
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis): A rare but serious complication resulting from high pressure in the small blood vessels of the lungs.
Hoarseness: Can occur if an enlarged pulmonary artery presses on the nerves in the chest.
